Boeing Unveils 777 ‘ecoDemonstrator’ to Advance Sustainable Aviation Technologies  

Boeing has introduced the newest iteration of its experimental test platform, the 777 “ecoDemonstrator,” as part of its ongoing program to develop and evaluate technologies aimed at reducing environmental impact and improving operational efficiency in commercial aviation. The unveiling, held in June 2022, showcased a suite of upgrades to the aircraft’s aerodynamics, systems integration, and materials, all designed to translate into tangible fuel savings and lower emissions in future passenger and cargo fleets.  

**Aerodynamic Enhancements**  
At the core of the ecoDemonstrator’s design improvements are modifications intended to reduce drag and optimize lift-to-drag ratios. Engineers have incorporated reshaped wing components, including adaptive trailing edge surfaces, which can adjust dynamically in flight to respond to varying aerodynamic conditions. These refinements are expected to yield incremental gains in fuel efficiency, which, when scaled across a fleet, could result in significant reductions in fuel burn over time.  

The test aircraft also features updated fairings and nacelle designs intended to smooth airflow around the fuselage and engine housings. By minimizing turbulent airflow and pressure differentials, the changes contribute to both reduced fuel consumption and lower noise levels during takeoff and landing.  

**In-Flight Testing Equipment**  
To validate the performance of these new systems, the ecoDemonstrator is outfitted with an array of advanced sensors and data acquisition tools. These include high-resolution pressure transducers, infrared thermography systems, and real-time telemetry links that allow engineers to monitor aerodynamic performance and structural loads during flight. The ability to collect and analyze such data in operational conditions enables rapid iteration of designs and more precise modeling of aircraft behavior under various environmental circumstances.  

Boeing’s test flights will encompass a variety of operational scenarios, including differing altitudes, speeds, and weather conditions, to ensure that the gathered data reflects the diverse realities of commercial aviation. This empirical approach is intended to shorten the development cycle for new technologies and facilitate earlier integration into production aircraft.  

**Innovative Materials and Systems**  
Another key focus of the ecoDemonstrator program is the evaluation of advanced materials aimed at both weight reduction and durability. The latest 777 platform incorporates composite components in secondary structures, as well as lightweight alloys in areas traditionally made from heavier metals. These substitutions are designed to maintain or improve structural integrity while lowering the aircraft’s overall mass, thereby improving fuel economy.  

The program is also testing next-generation cabin systems, such as improved environmental control units that use less energy to heat, cool, and ventilate the passenger cabin. Additionally, the aircraft is equipped with systems capable of running on a variety of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), allowing Boeing to assess performance and emissions profiles across different fuel blends.  

**Operational Cost and Environmental Benefits**  
Boeing projects that the combination of aerodynamic refinements, material innovations, and systems efficiencies could translate into measurable cost savings for operators. Reduced fuel consumption directly lowers one of the largest recurring expenses for airlines, while also decreasing greenhouse gas emissions per flight. Lower noise emissions can also help carriers comply with increasingly stringent airport noise regulations, potentially expanding operational flexibility at noise-sensitive airports.  

**Industry Context and Collaboration**  
The ecoDemonstrator program operates in collaboration with multiple stakeholders, including suppliers, research institutions, and regulatory bodies. Each test cycle involves partnerships to evaluate technologies that may have applications beyond Boeing’s own aircraft portfolio. By sharing certain findings with industry partners, Boeing aims to accelerate the adoption of effective sustainability measures across the aviation sector.  

While the 777 ecoDemonstrator is a testbed rather than a production model, its components and systems serve as precursors to features that could be incorporated into future commercial aircraft. The program’s iterative nature—testing, refining, and re-testing—ensures that only technologies with demonstrated operational benefits proceed toward certification and deployment.  

**Looking Ahead**  
Boeing’s unveiling of the 777 ecoDemonstrator underscores the company’s commitment to integrating sustainability into the design and operation of next-generation aircraft. As environmental performance becomes an increasingly important factor in airline fleet planning, technologies validated through programs like the ecoDemonstrator will play a critical role in shaping the industry’s path toward lower emissions and greater efficiency.  

The coming years will determine how swiftly and effectively such advancements can be scaled and implemented in the global fleet. In the meantime, the ecoDemonstrator continues to serve as a flying laboratory, gathering the data and operational experience necessary to inform the next wave of aviation innovation.

**Morning Light: A Simple Path to Better Health**  

There’s something quietly transformative about stepping outside in the early hours, when the world is still waking up and the sun’s first rays spill across streets, parks, and gardens. Beyond the peaceful atmosphere, science increasingly confirms that morning sunlight offers tangible health benefits. By incorporating outdoor morning walks into your routine, you can tap into the restorative effects of natural light—boosting vitamin D production, regulating your circadian rhythm, and enhancing mental well-being.  

---

### Vitamin D: Nature’s Morning Gift  

Vitamin D plays a crucial role in maintaining strong bones, supporting immune function, and reducing the risk of certain chronic illnesses. While it can be obtained through diet and supplements, the body’s most efficient source is sunlight. When ultraviolet B (UVB) rays reach your skin, they trigger vitamin D synthesis, a process that is particularly potent when the sun is lower in the sky and the light is less intense but still effective.  

Morning sunlight tends to carry a gentler UV index compared to midday, reducing the risk of overexposure while still providing enough UVB for your body to produce vitamin D. Just 15–30 minutes of outdoor walking in the morning, with hands and face exposed, can contribute significantly to meeting daily requirements—especially during spring and summer months.  

---

### Circadian Rhythm: Setting Your Internal Clock  

Your circadian rhythm is an internal 24-hour cycle that influences sleep-wake patterns, hormone release, digestion, and even mood. Light is the primary signal that keeps this rhythm aligned with the natural day-night cycle. Morning light, rich in blue wavelengths, sends a clear message to the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus: it’s time to be awake, alert, and active.  

Exposure to bright natural light soon after waking helps suppress melatonin production, the hormone that encourages sleep, and boosts cortisol levels in a healthy morning surge. This alignment can improve sleep quality at night, reduce daytime fatigue, and enhance overall energy. People who consistently get morning light often find it easier to fall asleep at a reasonable hour and wake feeling refreshed.  

---

### Mental Well-being: The Mood-Lifting Effect  

Beyond its physiological effects, morning sunlight exerts a profound influence on mental health. Studies have linked regular exposure to natural light with reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety, likely due to its role in stimulating serotonin production. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that contributes to feelings of happiness, calm, and focus.  

The act of walking outdoors also engages other mood-enhancing factors: gentle physical activity promotes endorphin release, fresh air encourages deeper breathing, and the visual stimulation of nature can reduce mental clutter. Whether you stroll through a neighborhood, a park, or along a waterfront, the sensory experience combined with morning light creates a natural uplift that can carry through the day.  

---

### Practical Ways to Incorporate Morning Walks  

Making morning walks a habit doesn’t require drastic lifestyle changes. Begin by setting aside 20–30 minutes soon after waking. Opt for routes that maximize sun exposure—open streets, waterfronts, or park trails without heavy tree cover. Even in cooler seasons, the light benefits remain, so dressing appropriately ensures you can maintain the routine year-round.  

Pairing your walk with another enjoyable activity can help cement the habit: listening to a favorite podcast, practicing mindfulness, or meeting a friend for a shared stroll. Over time, the combined effects of movement, fresh air, and sunlight become a cornerstone of daily health.  

---

### The Lasting Impact  

Morning sunlight is a free, abundant resource that aligns with the body’s natural design. Through the simple ritual of an outdoor walk, you invite in benefits that ripple across physical, mental, and emotional domains: stronger bones, better sleep, brighter mood, and a steadier daily rhythm.  

In a fast-paced world, these early moments in the sun offer not just health advantages, but also a pause—a gentle reminder that wellness often begins with something as simple as stepping outside and letting the day’s first light touch your skin.

**Advances in Biodegradable Medical Sutures: Polymer Blends for Enhanced Strength and Controlled Dissolution**  

**Abstract**  
Biodegradable sutures have transformed postoperative wound management by eliminating the need for suture removal and reducing infection risks. Recent developments in polymer chemistry have enabled the creation of suture materials with enhanced tensile strength, predictable dissolution timelines, and improved biocompatibility. This paper reviews the latest advances in biodegradable suture technology, with emphasis on novel polymer blends, their mechanical performance, and degradation kinetics under physiological conditions. Comparisons are drawn between traditional polyglycolic acid (PGA) and polylactic acid (PLA)-based sutures and emerging copolymer systems that incorporate polycaprolactone (PCL), trimethylene carbonate (TMC), and bioactive additives.  

**1. Introduction**  
Sutures are a critical component of surgical practice, serving to approximate tissue during healing. Biodegradable sutures offer distinct advantages over non-absorbable alternatives, including reduced patient discomfort, elimination of removal procedures, and minimized scarring [1]. Conventional absorbable sutures rely on homopolymers such as PGA, PLA, and polydioxanone (PDO), which degrade via hydrolysis of ester bonds. However, limitations remain in terms of premature loss of tensile strength, unpredictable degradation rates in variable tissue environments, and potential inflammatory responses to breakdown products [2].  

Recent research has focused on developing advanced polymer blends that address these limitations by tailoring crystallinity, molecular weight distribution, and hydrophilicity. Blends incorporating PCL, TMC, and other monomers allow fine control over degradation kinetics, while reinforcing agents and bioactive coatings can enhance tissue integration and healing outcomes [3].  

**2. Polymer Blends and Mechanical Enhancement**  
The tensile strength of biodegradable sutures must be maintained for a sufficient period to support tissue healing, typically ranging from 7 to 28 days depending on the surgical site [4]. PGA and PLA offer high initial strength but may lose integrity rapidly in moisture-rich environments. To mitigate this, blending with PCL—known for its slower degradation and flexibility—can extend strength retention without compromising biodegradability.  

Studies have shown that a 70:30 PGA:PCL blend retains over 50% of its tensile strength after two weeks in simulated body fluid, compared to less than 30% for pure PGA sutures under identical conditions [5]. Incorporation of TMC further improves elasticity and knot security, important factors in surgical handling. Nanofiller additives, such as hydroxyapatite nanoparticles, have also been explored to increase load-bearing capacity while promoting osteointegration in orthopedic applications [6].  

**3. Controlled Dissolution Rates**  
Optimizing dissolution rates is essential to match suture degradation with tissue regeneration timelines. Hydrolysis rates can be modulated through copolymer composition, chain branching, and surface modifications. For example, increasing PLA content in a PGA/PLA blend slows degradation due to PLA’s higher hydrophobicity and crystallinity [7].  

Surface treatments, including plasma etching and bioactive coatings, can further refine dissolution behavior. Coatings of chitosan or collagen not only adjust moisture absorption but also promote cellular adhesion and reduce local inflammatory responses [8]. Emerging approaches involve embedding enzymatically cleavable linkages within the polymer backbone, enabling site-specific degradation initiated by local tissue enzymes rather than solely by hydrolysis [9].  

**4. Biocompatibility Considerations**  
The breakdown products of biodegradable sutures—primarily lactic and glycolic acids—are metabolized via natural pathways but can cause localized pH shifts. Polymer blends incorporating buffering agents, such as calcium carbonate, have been shown to mitigate acid accumulation and maintain a more neutral microenvironment conducive to healing [10].  

Furthermore, the addition of bioactive agents, such as antimicrobial peptides or growth factors, into the suture matrix represents a promising strategy to enhance healing while reducing infection risk. These functionalized sutures must balance controlled release profiles with mechanical stability to remain clinically viable [11].  

**5. Conclusion**  
Advances in biodegradable medical sutures are increasingly driven by sophisticated polymer blending strategies that optimize mechanical strength, dissolution rates, and biocompatibility. The integration of PCL, TMC, nanofillers, and bioactive agents into traditional PGA or PLA matrices represents a significant step toward customizable suture systems tailored to specific surgical requirements. Continued interdisciplinary research between polymer chemists, biomedical engineers, and clinicians will be essential to translate these laboratory innovations into widespread clinical adoption.

The most invasive level of breathing support technology is used when the pulmonary system cannot sustain adequate ventilation. Medical ventilators literally breathe for the patient. They can be used invasively or non-invasively. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is relatively simple as ventilation is provided through a mask that is sealed to the nose and mouth externally. When NIV only provides one continuous pressure setting to a spontaneously breathing patient, this is called continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP); when there is one pressure for inhalation (IPAP) and a lower pressure for exhalation (EPAP) a respiratory rate is provide; this is called bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP), since there is a different pressure during inhalation and exhalation. NIV is indicated to help patients who can protect their own airway but need assistance oxygenating and/or ventilating. However, hospital ventilators as used in intensive care units (ICUs) commonly require the patient to be intubated wherein a breathing tube is inserted through the mouth or neck and into the trachea. During this invasive ventilation, the tubing is sealed off and the system periodically inflates the lungs. Breathing frequency and parameters to regulate tidal volume are set specifically for each patient.

This “O2 therapy” can be low- or high-flow. In low-flow O2 therapy, a small tube provides O2 enriched flow to a nasal cannula or mask from a cylinder or a portable O2 generator at up to 15 L per minute (LPM). Of note, low-flow O2 therapy can only deliver up to ~80% fraction of inspired oxygen. In high-flow O2 therapy, flows of more than 15 LPM are delivered to a mask or nasal cannula, typically through larger bore tubing. In low- and high-flow O2 therapy applications, the flow rates and O2 concentrations delivered are tailored to the needs of the patient.

**Advancements in Multi-Device Wireless Charging Technology Promise Safer, Faster Performance**  

*By TechPower News Desk*  

In recent years, the demand for convenient, cable-free charging solutions has grown rapidly, driven by the proliferation of smartphones, smartwatches, wireless earbuds, and other compact electronics. Now, a new generation of wireless charging pads is emerging that can power multiple devices at once, intelligently distributing current across all charging points to maintain efficiency and prevent overheating.  

**From Single-Coil to Multi-Point Systems**  
Traditional wireless charging pads have generally relied on one or two fixed coils, limiting their ability to charge more than one device at a time or requiring precise placement to ensure a steady connection. This constraint has often led to uneven charging speeds, inefficiencies, and heat buildup.  

The latest designs incorporate arrays of smaller, overlapping coils controlled by advanced power management chips. These systems can detect the position of each device on the pad, dynamically allocate current, and adjust coil activation in real time. The result is a platform that can charge three or more devices simultaneously without the performance drop-off or thermal issues that plagued earlier models.  

**Intelligent Power Distribution**  
One of the most notable innovations is the integration of current-balancing algorithms. Instead of delivering maximum available power to the first device placed on the pad — potentially starving others of adequate current — the new controllers continuously monitor each device’s charging state. They then allocate power proportionally, ensuring that all devices receive an optimal charge rate without exceeding safe thermal limits.  

This approach also extends component longevity. By preventing any single coil from operating at peak output for extended periods, the system reduces localized heat stress, which is a common cause of premature hardware failure in wireless chargers.  

**Thermal Management and Safety Enhancements**  
Overheating has been a persistent concern in wireless charging technology, as inductive power transfer inherently generates heat. The new multi-device pads employ a combination of passive and active cooling strategies. Heat-dissipating aluminum housings, strategically placed ventilation channels, and temperature sensors embedded near the coils work in concert to maintain safe operating conditions.  

If a hotspot is detected, the system can temporarily reduce output to that specific coil or shift the active charging zone to another coil in the array. This prevents damage to both the charger and the device batteries, while maintaining steady progress toward full charge.  

**Universal Compatibility and Standards Compliance**  
Another driver for adoption is the growing adherence to the Qi wireless charging standard, which ensures interoperability between chargers and devices from different manufacturers. The latest multi-device pads are fully Qi-certified, supporting both standard 5W charging and higher-output modes of 7.5W, 10W, and even 15W for compatible devices.  

Some models go further by incorporating adaptive charging profiles that can recognize proprietary fast-charge protocols from major smartphone brands, automatically adjusting voltage and current to match the device’s capabilities.  

**Design and User Experience**  
Manufacturers are also paying attention to aesthetics and ease of use. Sleek, low-profile designs with soft-touch surfaces reduce the risk of scratching device casings. LED indicators provide real-time feedback on charging status for each device, while companion mobile apps allow for firmware updates and customization of charging behaviors.  

Emerging features include programmable charging schedules — enabling users to delay charging until off-peak energy hours — and the ability to prioritize certain devices if needed. While these are still niche capabilities, they point toward a future in which wireless charging pads become more intelligent energy management tools rather than simple power accessories.  

**Market Outlook**  
Industry analysts forecast strong growth in the multi-device wireless charging segment over the next five years, fueled by the expansion of the smart home ecosystem and the trend toward reducing cable clutter. As component costs decline and efficiency improves, these advanced pads are expected to become mainstream, offering consumers a safer, faster, and more flexible way to keep their devices powered.  

With the combination of intelligent current distribution, robust thermal safeguards, and broad device compatibility, the newest generation of wireless charging pads represents a significant leap forward in consumer charging technology. For many users, this could mean the end of juggling multiple chargers — and a step toward a more seamless, cable-free future.

# FAQs How do mosquitoes get into my house? _Expand_ Mosquitoes are singularly adept at entering houses through any portal available, be it through broken window or door screens, attic soffits or through bathroom exhaust vents. A favorite resting spot is the garage, so take care to keep resting female mosquitoes from coming into the house through the garage. What can homeowners do to reduce mosquito bites? _Expand_ If possible, schedule your activities to avoid the times when mosquitoes are most active - usually dawn and dusk. You should also dress in light, loose-fitting clothing. If you have a deck, light it using General Electric yellow "Bug Lights". These lights are not repellant, per se, but do not attract mosquitoes like other incandescent lights. Mosquitoes are relatively weak fliers, so placing a large fan on your deck can provide a low-tech solution. Citronella candles have a mild repellent effect, but do not offer significantly more protection than other candles producing smoke. Are backyard misting systems effective? _Expand_ Scheduled sprays used by these misters may needlessly broadcast pesticides into the environment, affecting mosquitoes and non-target insects alike. Modern mosquito control strategies emphasize an integrated approach, based upon a profound knowledge of the target, so that's its various vulnerabilities can be exploited by the many tools we've developed for that purpose. Effective mosquito control requires continual survey of adult mosquito densities to determine if certain triggers for control are met. This reduces the use of adulticides to only those times when they are required. Do bug-zappers work? _Expand_ Black light insect electrocution devices (Bug Zappers, etc.) are purchased in huge quantities by homeowners due to their demonstrated ability to attract and kill thousands of insects over a 24 hr. period. One industry representative estimates that over 1.75 million of these devices are purchased annually in the U.S. But do they really control pest insects? Bug zappers do indeed kill some mosquitoes. However, the only two controlled studies conducted to date by independent investigators at the University of Notre Dame showed that mosquitoes comprised merely 4.1% and 6.4% respectively of the daily catch over an entire season. Even more important was the finding in both studies that there was no significant difference in the number of mosquitoes found in yards with or without bug zappers. What is particularly disconcerting, however, is the number of non-pest insects that comprise the vast majority of trap catch. Many of these insects are beneficial predators on other insect pests. They in turn constitute a major part of the diet of many songbirds. Indeed, reduced numbers of moth and beetle prey species have contributed significantly to the decline of songbird populations in many affluent suburbs. Insect electrocution devices undoubtedly bear some responsibility for this phenomenon. Mosquitoes continue to be more attracted to humans than to the devices. One study conducted in homeowners' backyards showed that of the insects killed by these devices, only 0.13% were female mosquitoes. An estimated 71 billion to 350 billion beneficial insects may be killed annually in the United States by these electrocuting devices. Do ultrasonic devices work? _Expand_ At least 10 studies in the past 15 years have unanimously denounced ultrasonic devices as having no repellency value whatsoever. Yet, consumers flock in droves to hardware stores to purchase these contraptions. Why? The discovery that mosquitoes locate mates in mating swarms via wing beat frequency generated a great deal of research into ultrasound as a potential source of environmentally-friendly control. Yet, all attempts to affect mosquito behavior by ultrasound have fizzled, despite enormous amounts of money spent upon research and development. To be sure, the clever, high-tech, and imperceptible (by humans) use of ultrasound proved to be an exceedingly effective marketing tool for the repeller manufacturers. Homeowners were urged to buy ultrasonic repellers and the like to rid their houses of pests without the need to inhale "even one breath of poisonous spray". This appeal to the public's chemophobia, while extremely effective in diverting attention away from proven preventive and control measures (and toward their repeller products), has undermined an unbiased review of the subject by consumers desperate for a clean, effective, nonchemical means of mosquito control. Unfortunately, no such miracle cure exists. A pioneering study testing five different ultrasonic devices against four mosquito species convincingly demonstrated that ultrasound in the 20-70 kHz range used by these devices had no effect on reorienting flight by female mosquitoes either toward or away from human subjects. Additional tests have shown that sound generators capable of a wide range of frequencies were also ineffective in repelling mosquitoes. The fact is that these devices just do not work - marketing claims to the contrary.

Materials such as starch, cellulose, wood, sugar and biomass are used as a
substitute for fossil fuel resources to produce bioplastics; this makes the
production of bioplastics a more sustainable activity compared to conventional
plastic production.  [51]  The environmental impact of bioplastics is often
debated, as there are many different metrics for "greenness" (e.g., water use,
energy use, deforestation, biodegradation, etc.).  [52]  [53]  [54]  Hence
bioplastic environmental impacts are categorized into nonrenewable energy use,
climate change, [ eutrophication ](/wiki/Eutrophication "Eutrophication") and
[ acidification ](/wiki/Freshwater_acidification "Freshwater acidification") .
[55]  Bioplastic production significantly reduces [ greenhouse gas emissions
](/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions") and decreases
non-renewable energy consumption.  [51]  Firms worldwide would also be able to
increase the [ environmental sustainability
](/wiki/Environmental_sustainability "Environmental sustainability") of their
products by using bioplastics  [56]

Although bioplastics save more nonrenewable energy than conventional plastics
and emit less greenhouse gasses compared to conventional plastics, bioplastics
also have negative environmental impacts such as eutrophication and
acidification.  [55]  Bioplastics induce higher eutrophication potentials than
conventional plastics.  [55]  Biomass production during industrial farming
practices causes nitrate and phosphate to filtrate into water bodies; this
causes eutrophication, the process in which a body of water gains excessive
richness of nutrients.  [55]  Eutrophication is a threat to water resources
around the world since it causes harmful algal blooms that create oxygen dead
zones, killing aquatic animals.  [57]  Bioplastics also increase
acidification.  [55]  The high increase in eutrophication and acidification
caused by bioplastics is also caused by using chemical fertilizer in the
cultivation of renewable raw materials to produce bioplastics.  [51]

Other environmental impacts of bioplastics include exerting lower human and
terrestrial [ ecotoxicity ](/wiki/Ecotoxicity "Ecotoxicity") and carcinogenic
potentials compared to conventional plastics.  [55]  However, bioplastics
exert higher aquatic ecotoxicity than conventional materials.  [55]
Bioplastics and other bio-based materials increase stratospheric [ ozone
](/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") depletion compared to conventional plastics; this is a
result of [ nitrous oxide ](/wiki/Nitrous_oxide "Nitrous oxide") emissions
during fertilizer application during industrial farming for biomass
production.  [55]  Artificial fertilizers increase nitrous oxide emissions
especially when the crop does not need all the nitrogen.  [58]  Minor
environmental impacts of bioplastics include toxicity through using pesticides
on the crops used to make bioplastics.  [51]  Bioplastics also cause carbon
dioxide emissions from harvesting vehicles.  [51]  Other minor environmental
impacts include high water consumption for biomass cultivation, soil erosion,
[ soil carbon ](/wiki/Soil_carbon "Soil carbon") losses and [ loss of
biodiversity ](/wiki/Loss_of_biodiversity "Loss of biodiversity") , and they
are mainly are a result of land use associated with bioplastics.  [55]  Land
use for bioplastics production leads to lost [ carbon sequestration
](/wiki/Carbon_sequestration "Carbon sequestration") and increases the carbon
costs while diverting land from its existing uses  [59]

Although bioplastics are extremely advantageous because they reduce non-
renewable consumption and GHG emissions, they also negatively affect the
environment through land and water consumption, using pesticide and
fertilizer, eutrophication and acidification; hence one's preference for
either bioplastics or conventional plastics depends on what one considers the
most important environmental impact.  [51]

Another issue with bioplastics, is that some bioplastics are made from the
edible parts of crops. This makes the bioplastics compete with food production
because the crops that produce bioplastics can also be used to feed people.
[60]  These bioplastics are called "1st generation feedstock bioplastics". 2nd
generation feedstock bioplastics use non-food crops (cellulosic feedstock) or
waste materials from 1st generation feedstock (e.g. waste vegetable oil).
Third generation feedstock bioplastics use [ algae ](/wiki/Algae "Algae") as
the feedstock.  [61]

**Transforming Recycled Materials into Decorative Garden Water Features**  

There’s something magical about the sound of water in a garden. Whether it’s a gentle trickle or a lively cascade, a well‑placed water feature can bring a sense of calm, movement, and visual interest to your outdoor space. Even more satisfying is the opportunity to create such features using recycled building materials, giving new life to items that might otherwise end up discarded. With a bit of creativity, you can design a piece that blends seamlessly into your landscaping while reflecting your personal style.

---

### Choosing the Right Location

Before gathering materials, consider the placement of your water feature. A shaded corner can create a serene retreat, while a spot near a seating area invites relaxation. Think about visibility from different angles—both from inside your home and from various points in the garden. The location will influence the size, shape, and style of the design, as well as the kind of recycled materials that will work best.

---

### Sourcing Recycled Materials

Recycled building materials not only reduce waste but also add character. Bricks from an old patio can be repurposed into a base or border. Weathered timber from dismantled decking can serve as rustic framing. Ceramic tiles, mismatched but colorful, can line the interior of a basin. Even salvaged metal elements—such as copper piping—can be integrated into spouts or decorative accents.

When sourcing, check local reclamation yards, online marketplaces, or community “freecycle” groups. Look for materials with interesting textures and patina; these imperfections often enhance the charm of a garden water feature.

---

### Designing for Aesthetic Flow

Water features can take many forms: a tiered fountain, a cascading wall, or a simple basin with a bubbling center. Use sketches to plan the arrangement, keeping in mind how recycled materials will fit together. For example, old stone slabs can be staggered to create gentle drops, allowing water to flow in a natural, meandering path. Broken pottery can be embedded along the edge for a mosaic effect.

Balance is key—combine heavier materials like stone or brick with lighter elements such as driftwood or wire mesh sculptures. This interplay of textures will make the feature visually engaging.

---

### Integrating into Landscaping

A water feature should feel like part of the garden’s ecosystem. Surround it with plantings that complement its style. Ferns and hostas work well with shaded, mossy stone designs, while ornamental grasses and flowering perennials suit brighter, more open spaces. Consider adding lighting for nighttime drama: small solar LEDs tucked among rocks can highlight the movement of water after dusk.

Pathways leading to the feature can be paved with reclaimed bricks or flagstones. This creates a sense of journey and frames the piece as a focal point. If space allows, incorporate seating nearby—perhaps a bench crafted from old timber beams—to encourage lingering.

---

### Assembly Tips

Start with a sturdy base. For in‑ground basins, recycled concrete slabs can form a stable foundation. If building above ground, stack bricks or stone securely, using gravel or sand to level layers. Waterproof liners made from repurposed pond liners or heavy‑duty tarpaulin can help contain the water.

For movement, small submersible pumps can be concealed within recycled containers, such as an old metal bucket or ceramic jar. Copper or steel piping from past plumbing projects can be adapted into spouts; polish them for shine or leave them weathered for a more rustic appeal.

---

### Maintenance and Longevity

Although recycled materials add charm, they may require extra care. Inspect for cracks in stone or brick that could affect structural integrity. Wooden elements should be treated or sealed to withstand moisture. Periodically clean out debris from the basin to keep water flowing smoothly and prevent blockages.

With proper attention, your creation will continue to delight for years, evolving as moss grows over stone or patina deepens on metal.

---

### Celebrating Sustainability and Beauty

Crafting a decorative water feature from recycled materials is more than a design project—it’s an act of environmental mindfulness. By reimagining the potential of discarded items, you reduce waste, conserve resources, and create something uniquely yours. Each salvaged brick or weathered plank carries a story, and together they form a centerpiece that enriches your garden’s spirit.

The gentle sound of water, framed by textures of reclaimed stone and timber, can transform an ordinary space into a sanctuary. With thoughtful planning and a willingness to experiment, you can merge sustainability with artistry, leaving a lasting impression on both your landscape and the planet.

Chinese researchers found that the greatest annual yields were obtained from three cuttings, which start at full bloom in mid-June. Comfrey yields are frequently reported on a fresh-weight basis, which exaggerates the yield potential of the crop due to its high moisture content. Comfrey forage averaged about 89% moisture in Minnesota trials (Table 1). Moisture content of comfrey forage is higher than in some legume and grass forages. For example, alfalfa cut in early bloom has 80% moisture and winter rye has 75 to 85% moisture when harvested between the tillering and boot stages. Annual dry-weight yields in Minnesota ranged from about 12 to 6 t/acre for four or five cuttings. However, on a fresh-weight basis, the same yields ranged from 13 to 61 t/acre. The low yields in 1979 and 1980 from the 1979 planting, compared to the higher yield obtained in 1980 from the 1979 planting that was not harvested in 1979, indicates that the crop plants need time to accumulate root reserves before intensive harvesting begins. Quaker comfrey may produce forage yields almost as high as those of alfalfa or orchardgrass when planted at the optimal spacing and rate of fertility. Comfrey requires the addition of nitrogen fertilizer to produce a high yield and protein content, while alfalfa produces high yields and protein content without addition of nitrogen fertilizer. Alfalfa and other forages can be established more cheaply than comfrey, since it is usually planted as root cuttings, especially at the close spacing needed for maximum yield. Comfrey, like other perennials, may be difficult to eradicate in order to plant other crops. The high moisture content and unpalatability for some livestock species make utilization of comfrey as a feed difficult. The presence of toxic alkaloids is also a problem. Advantages of comfrey are that it is very winterhardy in northern environments and could stabilize soil on erodible lands. It also produces fresh forage at a time of the year (spring, fall) when forage may be short from other sources. Controversy about the safety of comfrey for internal use continues. Occasional use of comfrey for variety in one's diet and medicinal purposes will probably continue. Nonetheless, comfrey should no longer be considered a crop that can be consumed by humans or animals with complete safety. It should be noted that consumption of comfrey is usually at lower levels than in toxicity research. Studies need to be conducted that involve the normal or low intake of comfrey for a proper evaluation of the health hazard to people or farm animals. Comfrey can be used externally as a medicinal herb for the allantoin content and as a crop for composting, mulching, or green manuring.

**Finding Peace in the Countryside: How Rural Living Nurtures the Mind**  

For many, the allure of rural life is more than just an aesthetic preference—it’s a deep-seated yearning for a slower pace, open skies, and a sense of connection to the land. While cities offer convenience and variety, they also carry a constant backdrop of noise, crowds, and hurried schedules. Rural environments, by contrast, present opportunities to engage with nature in a way that can profoundly influence mental well-being.  

### The Stress-Relieving Power of Open Spaces  

Research into environmental psychology consistently shows that natural settings can lower cortisol levels, the body’s primary stress hormone. In rural settings, people are surrounded by landscapes that invite pause and deep breathing—rolling fields, wooded trails, and quiet streams. Unlike urban parks, which are often bordered by traffic and high-rise buildings, rural green spaces immerse visitors in uninterrupted natural scenery. This immersion allows the mind to shift away from constant stimulation and toward restorative calm.  

One of the most immediate benefits people notice after spending time in the countryside is a reduction in mental clutter. Without the barrage of advertisements, sirens, and crowded sidewalks, the brain has room to process thoughts more slowly and deliberately. This deceleration can be especially beneficial for those recovering from burnout or chronic stress.  

### Creativity Flourishes Away from the Noise  

Beyond stress relief, rural environments can spark creative thinking. Artists, writers, and problem-solvers often find that stepping away from urban life gives them the mental space needed for fresh ideas to emerge. The absence of constant interruptions allows for deeper focus, while the variety of natural stimuli—changing seasons, diverse wildlife, shifting light—provides inspiration.  

Gardening, for example, is a common rural pastime that fosters creativity in unexpected ways. Planning a garden involves envisioning color palettes, textures, and spatial arrangements, much like designing a painting or composing a piece of music. Similarly, hiking along unfamiliar trails can encourage curiosity and exploration, prompting new perspectives that carry over into other parts of life.  

Birdwatching, too, offers a unique blend of mindfulness and problem-solving. Identifying species requires observation, patience, and pattern recognition, all of which stimulate the brain’s creative and analytical centers. Over time, these activities can lead to a more flexible and imaginative mindset.  

### Mental Health Gains from Rural Rhythms  

Extended time in rural areas often brings a shift in daily rhythms. Instead of being dictated by commutes, deadlines, and crowded schedules, days are shaped by natural cycles—sunrise and sunset, seasonal changes, and weather patterns. This alignment with nature’s tempo can improve sleep quality, stabilize mood, and reduce anxiety.  

Physical activity is naturally woven into rural life. Whether tending a vegetable patch, walking to a neighbor’s farm, or clearing a trail, movement becomes part of the day rather than an isolated workout. Regular, moderate exercise has well-documented benefits for mental health, including the release of endorphins and improved cognitive function.  

Social interactions in rural communities also tend to be more intentional. Neighbors may be fewer, but connections are often deeper, built on mutual support and shared experiences. This sense of belonging can act as a protective factor against depression and loneliness.  

### Cultivating Mindfulness Through Nature  

Perhaps one of the most profound psychological benefits of rural living is the ease with which it encourages mindfulness. In the countryside, moments of quiet are abundant—watching clouds drift over a hill, hearing the rustle of leaves, or feeling the texture of soil while planting seeds. These simple sensory experiences anchor attention to the present moment, reducing rumination and fostering emotional resilience.  

Mindfulness practices, when integrated into daily rural activities, can enhance self-awareness and promote a lasting sense of peace. For instance, hiking can be approached not just as exercise, but as a meditative practice, focusing on each step, each breath, and each detail of the surrounding landscape.  

### Conclusion  

The psychological benefits of rural living extend far beyond the absence of city noise. By engaging in activities like gardening, hiking, and birdwatching, individuals can experience reduced stress, heightened creativity, and improved mental health. Rural environments invite a slower, more intentional way of life—one that nurtures both the mind and spirit. For those seeking renewal, the countryside offers not just a change of scenery, but a profound shift in how we think, feel, and connect with the world.

**Harvesting Rain for Your Garden: Low-Cost DIY Systems That Work**  

For many home gardeners, water bills rise sharply in dry months, and municipal restrictions can make it difficult to keep plants healthy. Capturing and storing rainwater offers a sustainable, cost-effective way to irrigate without relying solely on treated tap water. With a few simple tools and materials, you can build a system that channels rain from your roof into storage barrels, filters out debris, and delivers clean water directly to your garden beds.  

---

### Why Rainwater Harvesting Matters  

Rainwater is naturally soft, free of many dissolved minerals found in groundwater, and generally ideal for most plants. By diverting runoff from your roof into a collection system, you reduce stormwater impact, conserve treated water, and create a reserve for dry spells. Even small-scale systems can significantly supplement your irrigation needs—especially for herbs, vegetables, and ornamental plants.  

---

### DIY Barrel Systems  

One of the simplest and most affordable setups is the rain barrel. These can be repurposed food-grade drums or purchased ready-made.  

**Basic components include:**  
- **Inlet**: A section of downspout redirected into the barrel, often fitted with a mesh screen to keep out leaves and insects.  
- **Overflow outlet**: Prevents flooding by diverting excess water away from foundations.  
- **Spigot or tap**: Allows easy filling of watering cans or connection to a garden hose.  

To build your own:  
1. Place the barrel on a stable, raised platform to improve water pressure.  
2. Cut an opening at the top to fit the downspout, securing a fine mesh or gutter guard over it.  
3. Install a brass or plastic spigot near the bottom using a bulkhead fitting to prevent leaks.  
4. Add an overflow pipe higher up, directing excess water to a safe drainage area or another barrel.  

Repurposed barrels can often be sourced for free or at low cost from local food manufacturers, provided they are thoroughly cleaned.  

---

### Roof Catchment Designs  

Your roof is the primary rainwater catchment surface. Maximizing its potential means ensuring clean gutters and efficient flow into your storage system.  

**Tips for effective catchment:**  
- Install gutter guards or leaf screens to reduce debris entry.  
- Use downspout diverters to control when water enters the barrel, allowing you to bypass collection during heavy pollen seasons or roof maintenance.  
- Position barrels near the most productive downspouts—often those with the largest roof area feeding into them.  

For larger gardens, consider linking multiple barrels in series using short lengths of hose or PVC pipe. This increases capacity without requiring a single large tank.  

---

### Simple Filtration Before Use  

While rainwater is generally clean enough for irrigation, removing debris before it enters the barrel helps maintain water quality and prevent clogging.  

**Low-cost filter options include:**  
- **Mesh screens** over downspout inlets.  
- **First-flush diverters**—small attachments that discard the initial runoff, which may contain dust, pollen, and bird droppings from the roof surface.  
- **Gravel or sand filters** placed inline for larger systems, which trap fine particles before storage.  

Periodic cleaning of filters and barrels ensures water remains fresh and odor-free.  

---

### Maintenance for Longevity  

A DIY rainwater system performs best with seasonal checks. Clear gutters of leaves, inspect seals and fittings for leaks, and flush barrels at least once a year to remove sediment. In colder climates, drain and store barrels before freezing temperatures to prevent cracking.  

---

### Bringing It All Together  

With a modest investment of time and materials, you can create a rainwater harvesting system tailored to your garden’s needs. By combining a well-designed roof catchment, sturdy storage barrels, and simple filtration, you’ll have a reliable source of irrigation water that reduces costs and environmental impact.  

Whether you choose a single barrel or a network of linked tanks, the principles remain the same: capture, store, and use rainwater efficiently. Over time, your plants—and your water bill—will show the benefits of this sustainable approach.

Did you know that several countries, such as the Maldives, Malta and the Bahamas, meet all their water needs through the desalination process—that is, they convert seawater to freshwater? Oceans cover 70 per cent of the planet. They provide nourishment for over three billion people and absorb 30 per cent of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere and 90 per cent of the heat from climate change. Increasingly, they are also providing freshwater for a burgeoning population. While there’s no shortage of seawater, it’s important to understand and monitor the impact of the rapidly growing number of desalination plants on the environment. Desalination is the process of removing salts from water and a by-product of the process is toxic brine which can degrade coastal and marine ecosystems unless treated. !DesalinationAl Kaluf desalination plant in Oman _Photo Credit: Starsend at English Wikipedia_ In most desalination processes, for every litre of potable water produced, about 1.5 litres of liquid polluted with chlorine and copper are created. When pumped back into the ocean, the toxic brine depletes oxygen and impacts organisms along the food chain. “Increased salinity and temperature can cause a decrease in the dissolved oxygen content, resulting in conditions called hypoxia,” says Manzoor Qadir, Assistant Director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH). This can harm organisms living on or in the bottom of a water body and translate into observable effects throughout the food chain. In addition, certain compounds (e.g. copper, chloride) used in the desalination pre-treatment process can be toxic to organisms in the receiving water, according to Qadir. Saudi Arabia (population 34 million) gets about 50 per cent of its drinking water from desalination. A 2018 United Nations study says there are now almost 16,000 desalination plants operating in 177 countries, producing a volume of freshwater equivalent to almost half the average flow over the Niagara Falls. However, the toxic brine which is usually dumped in the sea, risks contaminating food chains if left untreated. Rising water demands associated with population growth, increased water consumption per capita and economic growth, coupled with diminishing water supplies due to climate change and contamination, are exacerbating water scarcity in most world regions. The study says unconventional water resources, such as those resulting from desalination, are key to support Sustainable Development Goal 6 (to ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all), but that innovation in brine management and disposal is required: seawater desalination can extend water supplies beyond what is available from the hydrological cycle. **Challenges and opportunities** Brine production and high-energy consumption are key downsides of desalination. Disposal of toxic brine is both costly and associated with negative environmental impacts. “Our estimates reveal brine production to be around 142 million m3 /day, approximately 50 per cent greater than previous quantifications,” says the study. On a more positive note, many desalination plants are in areas with plenty of sunshine where solar power can provide a more sustainable energy solution. Research suggests there are also economic opportunities associated with brine, such as commercial salt, metal recovery and the use of brine in fish production systems. !DesalinationDesalination plants are not new. This picture of a desalination plant in Eilat, Israel, was taken in 1964. _Photo Credit: Moshe Pridan (Israel National Photo Collection)_ Desalination is currently concentrated in high-income and developed countries. For affordable and environmentally friendly systems to be rolled out in low-income and lower middle-income countries, technological innovations are necessary, along with innovative financial mechanisms to support the sustainability of desalination schemes, says the study produced by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH) Canada project on Unconventional Water Resources. **Concentrated brine is wastewater—we have the means to tackle it** Globally, 80 per cent of wastewater ends up in our seas, rivers, lakes, and wetlands. Under the Global Programme of Action for the Protection of the Marine Environment from Land-based Activities, UN Environment is working to prevent degradation from land-based activities, such as the operation of desalination plants. The Global Programme also hosts and acts as the secretariat for the Global Wastewater Initiative. This Initiative is getting people to move away from waste removal and towards resource recovery. It focuses on capacity-building and training, promotion of best practices and technologies, awareness raising and communication, and addressing data gaps. In March 2019, the United Nations Environment Assembly adopted a resolution on the protection of the marine environment from land-based activities. Among other things, Member States agreed to “enhance the mainstreaming of the protection of coastal and marine ecosystems in policies, particularly those addressing environmental threats caused by increased nutrient, **wastewater**, marine litter and microplastics in support of the 2030 Agenda as a framework for sustainable development.”

**Weaving with Willow: From Harvest to Garden Craft**  

There’s a simple, timeless pleasure in working with willow. Its supple branches have been shaped into everything from fishing traps to elegant arbors for centuries, and the process of preparing and weaving them connects the craftsperson deeply to the seasons. With careful cutting and respect for the plant’s natural cycles, willow can provide a renewable source of material for outdoor furniture, decorative fences, and a host of other garden structures.  

### Seasonal Cutting and Selection  

The quality of your willow work begins with the timing of the harvest. Traditionally, willow is cut during the dormant season—late autumn through the end of winter—when the sap has retreated into the roots. This period not only preserves the health of the plant but also yields rods that are less prone to splitting and quicker to dry evenly.  

Choose long, straight rods free from side shoots for weaving. Different willow varieties offer varying degrees of flexibility, color, and bark texture; a mix can lend visual depth to your finished piece. For outdoor furniture, sturdier rods form the frame, while thinner, more pliable ones are suited to the weaving itself.  

### Sustainable Harvesting Practices  

A well-managed willow bed can produce usable material year after year without depleting the plants. Cut rods close to the base, encouraging regrowth from the stool (the root crown). Rotate your cutting areas to allow sections to rest and regenerate. Avoid overharvesting from wild stands; instead, cultivate a dedicated plot or source from growers who follow sustainable practices.  

Leaving some older stems in place provides habitat for wildlife and supports the plant’s resilience. Additionally, returning trimmed leaves and offcuts to the soil as mulch can help maintain fertility.  

### Preparing Willow for Weaving  

Freshly cut willow can be used immediately while still green and flexible, but many craftspeople prefer to dry and then re-soak the rods. Drying allows for long-term storage and gives the artisan more control over the working season.  

To dry, bundle rods by size and store them upright in a sheltered, airy space out of direct sun. Once fully dry, they can be rehydrated before use by soaking in water—anywhere from a few hours to several days, depending on thickness. The rods are ready when they bend easily without cracking.  

### Building Outdoor Furniture  

When constructing garden chairs, benches, or tables, begin with a sturdy framework. This might be made from thicker willow poles lashed together or from another durable wood. The weaving is then worked around and through this frame.  

For seating surfaces, use a tight weave for comfort and stability. Start at one edge and work methodically to the other, keeping the weave consistent in spacing and tension. The natural flexibility of willow allows for subtle shaping, creating curves that can cradle the body.  

Finishing touches, such as trimming protruding ends and securing loose ends, not only enhance appearance but also improve durability. A coat of natural oil can help protect the piece from weathering, though many artisans prefer to let the willow age naturally to a silvery patina.  

### Creating Decorative Fences  

Woven willow fencing—sometimes called wattle—offers both function and charm in the garden. Begin by driving sturdy stakes into the ground at regular intervals, then weave long willow rods in and out between them. Alternate the direction with each successive rod to create a stable structure.  

The result is a living-looking barrier that can define spaces, support climbing plants, or shelter delicate seedlings from wind. Over time, the fence may settle and compact; adding fresh rods into the weave can extend its life for several seasons.  

### Care and Longevity  

Willow, being an organic material, will eventually weather and decay, especially in outdoor conditions. Positioning furniture and fences where they can dry out between rains will prolong their life. Seasonal inspection and maintenance—tightening loose weaves, replacing worn rods—will keep your creations functional and beautiful.  

Working with willow is as much about the process as the product. The annual rhythm of cutting, preparing, and weaving invites a mindful connection to the land and the materials at hand. With respectful harvesting and thoughtful craftsmanship, willow can be transformed into structures that enhance both garden and home, carrying forward a tradition that has endured for generations.

**Environmental Impacts of Anaerobic Digestion Versus Aerobic Composting for Municipal Food Scrap Management**  

**Abstract**  
The management of post-consumer food scraps within municipal waste systems poses significant challenges and opportunities for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and generating renewable energy. Two primary biological treatment methods—anaerobic digestion (AD) and aerobic composting—are increasingly employed to divert organic waste from landfills. This paper examines the comparative environmental impacts of these processes, with particular attention to methane emissions, carbon sequestration potential, and the role of energy recovery in municipal sustainability strategies. Drawing on recent life cycle assessments and operational data from urban waste facilities, the analysis highlights trade-offs between the two systems and identifies key parameters influencing their environmental performance.  

**1. Introduction**  
Food waste constitutes a substantial fraction of municipal solid waste streams, commonly ranging from 15–30% by weight in high-income urban areas [1]. Traditional landfill disposal of food scraps results in anaerobic degradation under uncontrolled conditions, producing methane—a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential approximately 28–34 times greater than CO₂ over a 100-year period [2]. To mitigate these impacts, municipalities have adopted controlled biological processing methods, notably aerobic composting and anaerobic digestion. While both approaches leverage microbial activity to transform organic matter, their operational environments and outputs differ markedly, influencing their respective environmental footprints.  

**2. Process Overview**  

**2.1 Aerobic Composting**  
Aerobic composting employs oxygen-rich conditions to facilitate the microbial breakdown of organic matter into a stable humus-like product. The process typically occurs in windrows, aerated static piles, or enclosed vessels, with temperatures maintained between 55–65°C to accelerate decomposition and ensure pathogen reduction. The primary outputs are carbon dioxide, water vapor, and mature compost suitable for soil amendment. Methane emissions from aerobic composting are minimal under well-managed conditions, though nitrous oxide emissions can occur due to incomplete nitrification-denitrification cycles [3].  

**2.2 Anaerobic Digestion**  
Anaerobic digestion processes food scraps in oxygen-free reactors, where consortia of microorganisms convert organic matter into biogas—a mixture of methane (50–70%) and CO₂—and digestate. The biogas can be combusted for heat and electricity or upgraded to biomethane for injection into natural gas grids, displacing fossil fuel use. Digestate may be applied to land as a nutrient-rich amendment after appropriate treatment. The controlled capture of methane in AD contrasts with uncontrolled landfill emissions, positioning AD as both a waste treatment and renewable energy generation technology [4].  

**3. Comparative Environmental Impacts**  

**3.1 Methane Emissions**  
Life cycle assessments indicate that aerobic composting produces negligible methane compared to AD, but the methane from AD is intentionally captured and utilized [5]. The net climate impact depends on the efficiency of biogas recovery and the displacement of fossil fuel-derived energy. Fugitive methane losses from AD systems—often in the range of 1–3% of total production—can offset some benefits if not properly managed [6].  

**3.2 Energy Recovery and Carbon Offsets**  
Aerobic composting does not yield direct energy products, though it contributes to carbon sequestration when compost is applied to soils, enhancing organic carbon stocks. In contrast, AD’s biogas can generate significant quantities of renewable energy; a typical municipal AD facility processing 50,000 tonnes of food scraps annually can produce approximately 20,000–25,000 MWh of electricity [7]. This energy recovery can offset fossil fuel use, yielding substantial greenhouse gas savings.  

**3.3 Nutrient Recycling and Soil Health**  
Both processes return nutrients to soils, but compost typically contains higher levels of stable organic matter, improving soil structure and water retention. Digestate from AD, while nutrient-rich, may require additional curing or composting to enhance stability and reduce odor before land application [8].  

**4. Operational Considerations**  
The selection between AD and aerobic composting in municipal contexts depends on factors such as existing infrastructure, climate, feedstock composition, and policy priorities. AD requires more complex and capital-intensive facilities but offers the dual benefits of waste stabilization and energy generation. Composting systems are generally simpler and less costly to implement, but their benefits are primarily agronomic rather than energetic.  

**5. Conclusion**  
Both anaerobic digestion and aerobic composting provide pathways for diverting food scraps from landfills, reducing uncontrolled methane emissions, and contributing to circular economy objectives. AD offers greater potential for renewable energy generation, contingent upon effective methane capture and utilization, while aerobic composting delivers stable organic amendments with minimal direct greenhouse gas emissions. Optimal municipal strategies may integrate both methods, leveraging their complementary strengths to maximize environmental benefits.

!raise green climatetech crowdfundingImage: Raise Green / Facebook Climate change is the biggest problem humanity has ever faced. Experts say it will take $1 trillion of clean energy investments each year for 30 years to avoid the worst that is yet to come. Still, this sector remains chronically underfunded, and the investments that do exist are limited to a few technologies and led by large VC firms in metropolitan areas. To change that, Raise Green, an investment marketplace for clean energy projects, announced this week it has launched its first crowdfunding platform, allowing virtually anyone with a bit of extra money to invest in green energy. Describing itself as a sort of “local and grassroots Green New Deal,” Raise Green aims to democratize the funding process for anyone who doesn’t want to wait for the government or larger financial institutions to act. It also helps individuals start their own projects. “While Raise Green is just one piece of a much more comprehensive solution to climate change, it also doubles as an avenue for communities and individuals to join hands together in building the future that we want. A future that is centered around just, equitable, and sustainable practices,” founders Franz Hochstrasser and Matt Moroney said in a joint blog post. “As we have seen with recent Black Lives Matter protests, the COVID-19 lockdown, and economic turmoil: unrest incited from massive collective action issues can be converted into meaningful action — and ultimately big change.” CEO Hochstrasser is a former energy and climate appointee under the Obama administration and COO Moroney, a data scientist, has more than 10 years of experience in the environmental and sustainability sector. Their company was nurtured by Greentown Labs, a climate tech startup incubator out of Somerville — the largest of its kind in the country. “If we’re going to drive meaningful, long-term change in the fight against the climate crisis, we need more people and more capital to get on board,” Greentown Labs CEO Emily Reichert said in a statement. “At a time when investment in climate action is so needed, we are excited to see Raise Green’s tremendous efforts lead to the launch of this platform.” Raise Green’s first offering — the National Energy Improvement Fund — helps residential and commercial buildings get energy efficient or carbon-reducing upgrades. Since the beginning of this crowdfund earlier this month, NEIF has received $46,000, bringing it nearly one-fifth closer to its end goal of $250,000. Ultimately, Raise Green wants to offer a wide variety of opportunities, where people can invest as little as $100 and as much as $100,000 into projects ranging from solar power and water, to electric vehicle charging stations and affordable housing. The company says it has more than 50 other projects in the pipeline.

The Autonomie tool models transmissions as a sequence of mechanical torque gains. The
torque and speed are multiplied and divided, respectively, by the current ratio for the selected
operating condition. Furthermore, torque losses corresponding to the torque/speed operating
point are subtracted from the torque input. Torque losses are defined based on a threedimensional efficiency lookup table that has as inputs: input shaft rotational speed, input shaft
torque, and operating condition.1083
The general transmission models are populated with characteristics data to model specific
transmissions. Characteristics data are typically provided in the form of tabulated data for
transmission gear ratios, maps for transmission efficiency, and maps for torque converter
performance, as applicable. The quantity of data needed depends on the transmission technology
being modeled. The characteristics data for these models was collected from peer-reviewed
sources, transmission and vehicle testing programs, results from simulating current and future
transmission configurations, and confidential data obtained from OEMs and suppliers.1084

**Choosing Woods and Natural Fibers for Outdoor Furniture: Performance, Beauty, and Care**  

When selecting materials for outdoor furniture, the interplay between durability, appearance, and upkeep is essential. Woods and natural fibers each bring distinct qualities to a design, and understanding their strengths and limitations helps ensure pieces that remain both functional and attractive over time.  

### Weather Resistance and Durability  

Outdoor environments expose furniture to rain, sun, wind, and fluctuating temperatures. Dense hardwoods such as teak, ipe, and eucalyptus are prized for their natural oils and tight grain structures, which resist moisture penetration and insect damage. Teak, for example, develops a silvery patina over time when left untreated, a sign of its resilience in humid and coastal climates.  

Other woods, like cedar and redwood, contain natural compounds that deter decay and repel insects. While softer than tropical hardwoods, they remain stable under varying conditions and are lighter to move around patios or gardens. Proper sealing extends their lifespan, especially in regions with heavy rainfall.  

Natural fibers, including rattan, cane, and certain palm-derived materials, offer flexibility and visual warmth. However, untreated fibers are vulnerable to mold and fraying when exposed to prolonged moisture. Many makers now use weatherproofed versions, coated or treated to withstand UV rays and humidity without losing their pliancy.  

### Aesthetic Qualities  

The choice of wood or fiber directly influences the mood and style of outdoor spaces. Teak’s rich golden-brown hue conveys a classic, timeless elegance, while eucalyptus often displays a subtle reddish tone that pairs well with modern designs. Cedar’s soft amber shades bring a rustic charm, complemented by its distinct aromatic scent.  

Natural fibers lend a relaxed, organic feel, ideal for lounge chairs, daybeds, and woven accents. Rattan’s intricate patterns create visual interest, and its light color can be easily stained or painted to suit varying palettes. Combining hardwood frames with woven fiber seats balances structural strength with tactile softness, offering both comfort and visual depth.  

### Maintenance Requirements  

Even the most durable materials benefit from regular care. Hardwoods generally require minimal maintenance if allowed to weather naturally, but periodic cleaning with mild soap and water removes dirt and debris. For those preferring to maintain the original color, annual applications of specialized oils or sealants help preserve the wood’s luster.  

Cedar and redwood may be left unfinished for a silvery-gray look or sealed to enhance their natural tones. They are more prone to surface checking if neglected, so seasonal inspections and touch-ups are advisable.  

Natural fibers demand a gentler approach. Vacuuming or brushing loose debris prevents buildup, and occasional wiping with a damp cloth keeps surfaces fresh. Weatherproofed fibers can handle more exposure, but storing woven pieces under cover during heavy rain or snow greatly extends their life. Cushions and textiles paired with these materials should be made from outdoor-grade fabrics to resist fading and mildew.  

### Blending Materials for Optimal Performance  

Many outdoor furniture designs combine woods and fibers to leverage the strengths of each. A hardwood frame provides stability against wind and wear, while woven panels add breathable comfort. In climates with intense sunlight, pairing UV-resistant fibers with shade-providing fabrics reduces heat absorption and prolongs material integrity.  

Designers also mix species strategically: for example, using teak for tabletops and cedar for supporting elements to balance cost, weight, and durability. These combinations allow for tailored solutions that meet specific environmental demands without sacrificing style.  

### Conclusion  

Selecting the right woods and natural fibers for outdoor furniture involves weighing weather resistance, aesthetic appeal, and maintenance needs. Durable hardwoods like teak and ipe offer longevity in harsh conditions, while cedar and redwood provide lighter, aromatic alternatives. Weatherproofed natural fibers contribute comfort and texture, especially when combined with sturdy wood frames. By understanding the inherent qualities of these materials, makers and homeowners can create outdoor spaces that remain inviting and resilient for years to come.

You will probably be familiar with thermostats from central heating systems. These help maintain a steady temperature in the house by detecting the air temperature, and turning the heaters on and off depending on whether it is too hot or cold. The thermostat for your water cylinder works in much the same way. Instead of checking air temperature, it senses the water temperature at a certain point in the cylinder. When the water cools below the set temperature the thermostat turns on the element, bringing up the overall temperature.

# Weeding with Geese **Weeder geese are used with great success to control and eradicate troublesome grass and certain weeds in a variety of crops and plantings, according to Glenn Geiger and Harold Biellier of the Department of Animal Sciences at the University of Missouri.** The geese eat grass and young weeds as quickly as they appear, but do not touch certain cultivated plants. Why do geese eat certain plants with relish while showing no interest whatsoever for others? Perhaps only a goose knows the answer. Nevertheless, farmers throughout the country take advantage of this unusual characteristic. Geese work continuously from daylight to dark, seven days a week (even on bright, moonlit nights) nipping off the grass and weeds promptly as new growth appears. Geese remove grass and weeds next to plants that cannot be removed by hoeing or cultivation. Roots of the cultivated plants are not damaged as is so often the case with hoeing and machine cultivating. Geese also keep fence rows and irrigation ditches clean and work when the ground is too wet to hoe or cultivate. Proper use of geese can practically eliminate the need to hoe and pull grass and weeds. Expensive hand labor is replaced. The University of Tennessee Agricultural Experiment Station reports that using geese in cotton fields can save of $35 or more per acre. This figure does not take into account costs of management and salvage value of geese at the end of the season. Similar savings appeared when weeder geese were compared with dalapon as a weed control treatment. Clean fields mean increased yields, higher quality yields and easier harvesting. Geese are "manure spreaders" as well as "cultivators". They continually add fertilizer and organic matter to the soil. ### How to Use Weeder Geese In general, weeder geese should be placed in the fields or plantings early in the season when grass and weed growth first starts to appear. Under average conditions, two to four geese per acre are enough in row plantings. Usually no more than four geese per acre should ever be needed if they are put into fields when the first grass appears in spring. More may be required where plantings are in beds, since beds have a larger area where grass and weeds can grow. More geese also may be required if grass and weed infestation is heavy during wet seasons, or if grass and weeds have made considerable growth before geese are placed in the fields. White Chinese geese are the favorites for weeding purposes, or Africans where a larger bird is desired for marketing at the end of the weeding season. These geese are more active and energetic than Toulouse and Emden, although those breeds are also used. ### Management in the Field Brood day-old goslings to six to eight weeks of age before placing them in fields permanently without shelter. Younger birds can be used if they are brought into shelter at night or in event of rain. Goslings can be turned out on grass within a few days and supplemental feeding of grain started the second week. Water troughs should be placed in fields at the far end of rows so that geese will work the full length of rows on their way to drink. Water containers may be moved occasionally to make birds concentrate their efforts where they are most needed. If there are no trees in the field, provide temporary structures for shade. A common practice is to place cotton trailers in fields for this purpose. Small amounts of supplemental feed must be provided. The amount required usually will range from 5 to 20 pounds a day per 100 birds. You have to learn the proper amount to feed through experience. Geese must have sufficient appetite to graze well, but at the same time they must be maintained in a strong, active condition. Growing-mash pellets should be used as supplemental feed until at least 12 weeks of age. After this age, grain may be used if preferred. However, a small amount of chicken and turkey grower pellets (non-medicated) are recommended. Feed should be provided once per day in the evening and scattered so all birds will have an opportunity to pick up their share. High fences are not required, since geese seldom fly. A 24- to 30-inch fence is sufficient. Poultry netting supported by stakes often is used where temporary fencing is desired. It is claimed that electric fencing will keep foxes and dogs out of fields. Provide protection from foxes and stray dogs. Animals seldom attack during the day, so bring geese into a tight pen at night or use lights or flares where geese congregate at night. Some insecticides are poisonous to geese, so remove geese from the field during spraying and do not return them for several days. In case of rain, do not return weeders to the field until puddles where insecticides may collect have soaked into the ground. Herbicides apparently are not harmful. ### Marketing If weeders are to be sold on a weight basis at the end of season, bring geese in from fields and place them in the pen for fattening. Feed birds all the grain they will consume three or four times daily. Continue for three or four weeks until geese weigh 10 to 12 pounds or more. Growing mash or fattening pellets must be fed with grain for efficient feed conversion. Markets are highest during the four to six weeks before Thanksgiving and Christmas. Well-finished Emden, Toulouse and African geese are in best demand. Contact a poultry buyer or processor near you and arrange marketing details. Carrying geese over from one season to the next is not recommended. Older geese are less active in hot weather than young birds. Adult geese will eat more Johnsongrass roots turned up during tillage than goslings, but are more difficult to restrain from crossing fences. It is usually less expensive to buy goslings in the spring than to carry old birds through the winter.
