Which the average range of an electric bus? This is one of the main questions that public transport operators and authorities are asking themselves when they are dealing with a product, the battery-electric bus, which does not yet have a sufficient track record to allow certain evidence. Certainly, it is known that the range of an electric bus is influenced by the outside temperature, the use of air conditioning systems and, above all, heating. Last but not least, the driving behavior is decisive as well. On the basis of the information gathered so far, let’s try to sum up what we can outline on the topic: **how much does an electric bus consume?** !electric bus range consumption Empiric figures. Electric bus range with 18-meter vehicles ---------------------------------------------------------- Empiric figures come from the Ebus Test yearly held in Germany under the coordination of the specialized magazine Omnibusspiegel. In 2018, the test focused on 18-meter articulated buses . Three manufacturers took up the challenge: Bozankaya Sileo, Solaris, VDL. Following three days of tests in real operations condition on Bonn’s streets, the Ebus Test team measures the consumption of the vehicles, used to provide an average value between the competitors. ### Articulated electric bus range around 200 km (no heating) Then, which was the result? Consumption was **between 1.65 and 1.84 kilowatt hours per kilometer**. Heating off but air conditioning on. Around 20 per cent of losses during charging operation should be taken into consideration. Based on this data, **a 18-meter bus with 350 kWh of capacity can cover a range between 190 and 210 kilometres**. And what about 12-meter e-buses range? (in winter) -------------------------------------------------- Followingly, in 2019 the focus of Ebus Test was on 12-meter buses . This time, there were seven contenders on the starting blocks. The calculation of electric bus consumption was not easy, as temperatures were slightly above zero, so a considerable amount of the energy consumed went to heating. Also, not all vehicles were charged under the same conditions: some charging stations were located indoors, others outdoors. !electric bus range Adding another bit to an already diversified mix, buses with a diesel-fuelled auxiliary heating system consumed less power than those whose ambient temperature control is entirely battery-powered. As is natural, diesel and power consumption levels are inversely proportionate to each other. ### Power consumption of electric buses, a real test So, these were the results: **vehicles heated with the help of an auxiliary fossil fuel heater consume from 110.5 kWh plus 20 litres of fuel to 144 kWh plus 6.4 litres**. Power consumption **on buses with full-electric heating, “diluted” over 100 km, stands in the range between 179 and 235 kWh**. In other words, consumption is reported to span between 1 and 1.4 kWh/km on buses with fossil fuelled heating systems, and up to 2.35 on electrically heated ones. That is to say: **taking as a sample a solobus with (considerable) battery capacity of 300 kWh, range of the electric bus varies from 214 to 300 if diesel-heated and as low as 130 km if electrically-heated**. A huge difference. Electric bus range emerges from data ------------------------------------ A few hints on this topics come from an interview we had with Viriciti COO and co-founder **Alexander Schabert**. ViriCiti is a Dutch telematics company founded as a startup in 2012 with the mission of providing fleet management platforms to operators, particularly with regards to electric buses. The data collected by the company can be useful to determine which is the average consumption of electric buses, and therefore their range on one charge. !electric bus range _«On average, **a 12-meter bus has in the best conditions a consumpion of 0,8 kWh per km** – Shabert said -. We are talking of operations in a **normal day with 20 degrees, no much traffic and a skilled driver**. Everything depends on the heating. A bus operating in the winter, for instance at minus 10 degrees, with electric heating turned on **can reach a consumption of 2,3 – 2,5 kWh per km**. With diesel heating it could be 1,5»._ Making a quick calculation, based on the figures provided by ViriCiti, a sample 12-meter battery-electric bus with 300 kWh of battery capacity can cover, in the best days of the year, as many as 375 km. But **on a winter day, the mileage decrease to a figure between 120 and 130 km, is electrically heated**. Diesel heating allow a 200 km range. The importance of driver for the electric bus range --------------------------------------------------- Still Alexander Schabert from ViriCiti told us: _«We see about **30 per cent impact from the driving behaviour**. Drivers that don’t use regeneration because they push the brakes hard, and this activates directly the mechanical brake, regenerate only 5 per cent. But **if the driver use regeneration he can achieve 35 to 40 per cent regeneration**»._ Cold weather and electric bus range. CTE’s answer ------------------------------------------------- !electric bus range cold With regards to the impact of cold weather on the electric bus range, a study by CTE in late 2019 (realized in the US and funded **under a National Fuel Cell Bus Program grant** ) showed that the switch to cold temperatures (between -5 and 0° C) affects the range of up to 38 per cent decrease in case of battery-electric buses, and up to 23 per cent decrease for hydrogen-powered buses. The study have been carried on by the **Center for Transportation and the Environment (CTE)**, a nonprofit organization with a mission to improve the health of our climate and communities by bringing people together to develop and commercialize clean, efficient, and sustainable transportation technologies.

**Optimizing Thermostat Settings for Winter Comfort and Efficiency**  

As winter approaches, homeowners often seek to balance warmth with energy efficiency. The thermostat, central to any heating system, plays a key role in achieving this balance. Yet the optimal setting depends not only on personal comfort but also on the physical characteristics of the home—especially its floorplan and insulation quality.  

**Understanding How Thermostats Control Heating**  
Modern central heating systems rely on thermostats to regulate indoor temperature by cycling the boiler or furnace on and off. A thermostat set too high will cause the system to run longer and more frequently, consuming more energy. Conversely, a setting too low may leave rooms uncomfortably cool, prompting occupants to use supplementary heating devices. The goal is to find a temperature that maintains comfort across the home without unnecessary energy expenditure.  

**The Role of Floorplan Layout**  
One of the most overlooked factors in thermostat efficiency is the home’s layout. In open-plan designs, warm air circulates freely between spaces, allowing a single thermostat to maintain even temperatures with relative ease. This can mean the thermostat can be set at a slightly lower temperature without sacrificing comfort, as heat distribution is more uniform.  

In contrast, homes with segmented rooms or multiple stories present a challenge. Heat tends to rise, so upper floors may be warmer than lower ones. If the thermostat is located in a warmer area, it may shut off the heating before cooler rooms have reached the desired temperature. In these cases, zoning—using multiple thermostats or programmable radiator valves—can improve efficiency by tailoring heat delivery to each space’s needs.  

**Insulation and Heat Retention**  
Insulation quality is another critical component. Well-insulated walls, ceilings, and floors slow the rate at which heat escapes, allowing a thermostat to maintain a steady temperature with less frequent heating cycles. Double-glazed windows, insulated doors, and draught-proofing can significantly reduce heat loss, meaning the thermostat can be set lower without discomfort.  

Poor insulation, on the other hand, forces the heating system to work harder to compensate for rapid heat loss. In such homes, even an optimally set thermostat may result in high energy bills. Addressing insulation issues often yields greater efficiency gains than any thermostat adjustment alone.  

**Strategies for Optimal Settings**  
For most households, a steady, moderate thermostat setting during occupied hours—combined with a programmed setback during sleeping or unoccupied periods—offers the best balance between comfort and cost. Programmable thermostats or smart models can automate these changes, ensuring the heating system runs only when needed.  

Placement of the thermostat is equally important. It should be located away from direct sunlight, draughts, and heat sources, ideally in a central living area that reflects the average temperature of the home. This placement helps prevent false readings that could cause over- or under-heating.  

**Seasonal Adjustments and Monitoring**  
During the coldest months, small incremental increases—rather than large jumps—in thermostat settings can help maintain efficiency. Monitoring actual room temperatures with separate thermometers can reveal whether the thermostat setting is achieving the desired effect throughout the home.  

Additionally, homeowners should consider the interplay between central heating and supplemental sources. Fireplaces, space heaters, or underfloor heating can influence thermostat readings and may allow for lower central heating settings when used strategically.  

**Conclusion**  
The most efficient thermostat setting is not a fixed number but a balance point shaped by the home’s layout and insulation. By understanding these factors and making thoughtful adjustments, residents can enjoy a warm, comfortable winter while keeping energy consumption in check. A combination of proper thermostat placement, consistent moderate temperatures, and attention to insulation will yield the greatest returns in both comfort and cost savings.  

Ultimately, efficiency comes from viewing the thermostat as part of a larger system—one influenced by the physical structure of the home and the habits of its occupants. When these elements are aligned, winter heating can be both cozy and economical.

**Report: Adaptation Strategies of Urban Water Treatment Plants to Increased Industrial Wastewater Loads – Case Studies from Northern California**  

---

**Abstract**  
Urban water treatment plants are facing mounting challenges in managing increased volumes and complexity of industrial wastewater. This report examines adaptation strategies implemented by municipalities in Northern California, where diverse industrial growth and regulatory pressures have necessitated infrastructure upgrades, process innovations, and cross-sector collaboration. Through case studies in San Francisco, Oakland, and Sacramento, the analysis highlights technological interventions, policy frameworks, and operational adjustments that enable treatment facilities to meet stricter discharge standards while maintaining resilience against fluctuating industrial inputs.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Industrial wastewater composition varies widely depending on the sector, encompassing organic loads, heavy metals, complex chemical compounds, and high-temperature effluents. In Northern California, the expansion of biotechnology, food processing, and advanced manufacturing has intensified the burden on municipal treatment systems. Regulatory agencies, notably the California State Water Resources Control Board, have tightened effluent quality requirements, compelling urban plants to adapt both their hardware and operational protocols. This report outlines these adaptations, focusing on the interplay between technological upgrades, regulatory compliance, and collaborative governance.

---

**2. Background and Drivers of Change**  
Over the past decade, industrial activity in metropolitan regions such as San Francisco and Oakland has shifted toward higher-value, specialized production. This shift has led to:  

- **Increased pollutant diversity**: Biopharmaceutical effluents with complex organic molecules; electronics manufacturing introducing trace metals and solvents.  
- **Higher peak load variability**: Seasonal surges from food and beverage industries, episodic discharges from construction-related dewatering.  
- **Regulatory tightening**: Enforced lower thresholds for contaminants such as copper, mercury, and nitrogen compounds.  

These factors have strained conventional activated sludge processes, necessitating advanced treatment modules and more precise monitoring.

---

**3. Case Study: San Francisco Public Utilities Commission (SFPUC)**  
In response to increased industrial discharge from the biotechnology corridor, SFPUC invested in membrane bioreactor (MBR) systems at its Southeast Treatment Plant. The MBR installation improved removal rates for complex organics and reduced nutrient loads before discharge into the bay. Additionally, SFPUC implemented a Pretreatment Program requiring industrial clients to install on-site neutralization and filtration systems, thereby reducing the burden on municipal facilities. Real-time monitoring sensors now track influent composition, enabling rapid process adjustments.

---

**4. Case Study: East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD), Oakland**  
EBMUD’s adaptation strategy centered on upgrading secondary treatment capacity and introducing tertiary filtration using granular activated carbon (GAC) to address trace organic contaminants from local manufacturing. The district also expanded its industrial permitting and inspection program, incorporating predictive analytics to forecast load variations. A notable innovation was the integration of anaerobic digesters that process high-strength industrial waste into biogas, offsetting plant energy consumption.

---

**5. Case Study: Sacramento Regional Wastewater Treatment Plant (SRWTP)**  
Sacramento’s industrial profile includes food processing and agricultural product refinement, both of which produce high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) loads. SRWTP upgraded its aeration systems to fine-bubble diffusers, increasing oxygen transfer efficiency and reducing energy costs. The plant also piloted advanced oxidation processes (AOP) to break down persistent organic pollutants. Coordination with upstream industries through waste minimization workshops has reduced pollutant loads by fostering process changes at the source.

---

**6. Policy and Governance Implications**  
Successful adaptation in these municipalities has hinged on:  

- **Strong regulatory frameworks** enforcing pretreatment and discharge limits.  
- **Industry-municipality partnerships** that share data and invest jointly in mitigation measures.  
- **Flexible funding mechanisms**, including state revolving funds and public-private partnerships, to finance capital-intensive upgrades.  

The case studies underscore that technological interventions alone are insufficient; governance models that encourage compliance and innovation are equally critical.

---

**7. Conclusions**  
Northern California’s urban water treatment plants demonstrate a range of adaptive strategies to meet the challenges of increased industrial wastewater loads. Investments in advanced treatment technologies, proactive pretreatment requirements, and collaborative governance have improved contaminant removal efficiency, reduced operational risks, and enhanced environmental protection. As industrial profiles continue to evolve, ongoing monitoring, adaptive capacity building, and sustained funding will be essential to maintain compliance and protect public water resources.

---

Mastercard today announced it is accelerating efforts to remove first–use, PVC plastics from payment cards on its network by 2028. This initiative further reinforces the company’s sustainability commitments and scales the accessibility of more sustainable card offerings for consumers seeking a way to reduce the environmental impact of their wallet. In a first move for a payment network, from January 1, 2028, all newly–produced Mastercard plastic payment cards will be made from more sustainable materials – including recycled or bio-sourced plastics such as rPVC, rPET, or PLA1 \- and approved through a certification program. The company will support its global issuing partners through the transition away from virgin PVC. “The world has a plastic problem. Solving it will be a whole-of-society task, yet efforts are often taken in isolation or without coordination,” **said** **Sandeep Malhotra, Executive Vice President, Products & Innovation, Asia Pacific, Mastercard**. With this sustainable cards effort, Mastercard is bringing its global network of banks, financial institutions and consumers – who collectively hold more than 3 billion Mastercard cards – together to build a greener payments sector through collaboration and partnership.” Mastercard launched its Sustainable Card Program in 2018. Since then, over 330 issuers across 80 countries have voluntarily signed up, including 90 issuers in 15 markets2 across the Asia Pacific region. Since then, Mastercard has been working in partnership with major card manufacturers to transition more than 168 million cards across its network, including 31 million in the Asia Pacific region, to recycled and bio-based materials. **Turning Grey Water into Garden Gold: A Step-by-Step Guide to Low-Cost Irrigation Reuse**  

Grey water—wastewater from showers, kitchen sinks, and laundry (excluding toilet waste)—can be a valuable resource for home gardeners when treated and reused responsibly. Repurposing this water for irrigation reduces household water demand, helps conserve fresh water supplies, and can be accomplished on a modest budget. In this post, we’ll walk through simple, affordable methods for converting grey water into safe, non-potable irrigation water, along with practical tips for keeping your plants healthy.  

---

### Understanding Grey Water and Its Uses  

Grey water contains soap residues, small amounts of grease, and traces of dirt or organic matter. While it is not safe for drinking, it can be suitable for watering ornamental plants, fruit trees, and certain edible crops (with precautions). The key is to remove solids, reduce contaminants, and ensure that the water is applied in a way that does not touch edible plant parts directly.  

---

### Step 1: Source Separation  

The first step is to identify and separate grey water sources from black water (toilet waste). This can be as simple as routing water from a laundry machine’s outflow hose or collecting shower water in a basin. Avoid water from dishwashers or heavily greasy kitchen sinks if possible, as these tend to have higher concentrations of fats and food particles.  

---

### Step 2: Primary Filtration  

A basic filtration stage removes hair, lint, and larger particles. You can create a low-cost filter using:  

- **A bucket and mesh screen**: Fit a fine mesh or nylon stocking over the mouth of a bucket and pour the grey water through it.  
- **Gravel and sand layers**: Set up a small drum or large container with layers of coarse gravel at the bottom, followed by fine sand above. As the water passes through, solids remain trapped.  

These methods are inexpensive and require minimal technical skill. Clean or replace the filter media regularly to prevent clogging and odor buildup.  

---

### Step 3: Secondary Treatment for Garden Safety  

Once solids have been removed, the water can be run through a secondary treatment stage to reduce odors and improve quality for plants. Options include:  

- **Charcoal filtering**: Activated charcoal can absorb certain organic compounds and odors. You can purchase it in bulk for aquarium use and place it in a mesh bag within the water flow path.  
- **Settling tanks**: A small barrel or drum allows fine particles to settle out over several hours before water is drawn for irrigation.  

These steps improve the clarity and smell of the water, making it more pleasant to handle and safer for soil health.  

---

### Step 4: Safe Distribution to Plants  

Grey water should be applied directly to the soil, not sprayed onto leaves or edible parts of plants. A simple gravity-fed drip line or perforated hose buried under mulch works well. This minimizes contact with plant surfaces and reduces the chance of bacterial contamination.  

For edible crops, apply grey water only to the base of fruit trees or plants where the edible portion grows above ground and does not touch the soil directly. Avoid using it on root vegetables.  

---

### Step 5: Maintenance and Monitoring  

To keep your system running smoothly:  

- **Rotate application areas** to prevent salt or detergent buildup in the soil.  
- **Use plant-safe soaps and detergents** that are biodegradable and low in sodium or boron.  
- **Flush with fresh water** periodically to dilute any accumulated residues.  

Monitor plant health—yellowing leaves or stunted growth may indicate that the soil chemistry needs adjustment.  

---

### Cost-Saving Tips  

- Repurpose old barrels, buckets, and hoses instead of buying new.  
- Collect sand and gravel from local suppliers or leftover construction projects.  
- Share bulk purchases of filter media with neighbors.  

---

### Final Thoughts  

By following these steps, you can transform household grey water into a valuable irrigation resource without expensive equipment or complex systems. The key is to keep the process simple, maintain your filters, and use plant-friendly products in your home. With a little effort, your garden can thrive while reducing your environmental footprint and water bills.  

---

**Title:**  
Design Ergonomics in Public Playground Equipment: Safety Standards, Accessibility, and Injury Prevention  

**Abstract**  
The design of public playground equipment requires careful integration of ergonomics to ensure safety, accessibility, and injury prevention for diverse user groups. This review synthesizes existing literature on ergonomic principles applied to playground design, with emphasis on compliance with safety standards, inclusive design for children with varying abilities, and strategies to reduce injury risks. Findings indicate that adherence to established guidelines, combined with innovative inclusive features, can significantly improve user experience while minimizing hazards. Implications for designers, municipal planners, and policymakers are discussed.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Playgrounds serve as critical environments for physical activity, social interaction, and developmental learning among children. The ergonomics of playground equipment—defined here as the applied science of optimizing design to fit users’ physical and cognitive capabilities—is central to promoting safe and accessible use. Poor ergonomic design can lead to increased injury rates, reduced usability for certain populations, and diminished developmental benefits. This paper reviews the current state of design ergonomics in public playgrounds, focusing on safety standards, user accessibility, and injury prevention.  

---

**2. Safety Standards in Playground Design**  
International and national safety standards, such as those outlined by ASTM F1487 and EN 1176, provide baseline requirements for playground equipment design. These standards address structural integrity, surfacing materials, fall height limitations, and spacing between components to prevent entrapment hazards [1]. Ergonomic considerations intersect with these standards in the sizing of equipment relative to age groups, ensuring that handles, steps, and seats are proportionate to children’s anthropometric measurements. Regular safety audits and maintenance schedules further reinforce compliance and reduce accident probability.  

---

**3. Ergonomic Approaches to Accessibility**  
Accessibility in playground design is increasingly guided by universal design principles, which advocate for environments usable by people of all ages and abilities without the need for adaptation. Ergonomic solutions include ramps with appropriate gradients, transfer platforms for wheelchair users, and sensory panels positioned at reachable heights for seated children [2]. The spatial arrangement of equipment should allow for unobstructed pathways and facilitate supervision by caregivers. Inclusive playgrounds incorporate multi-sensory experiences—such as textured surfaces, auditory elements, and visual cues—that engage children with varying sensory profiles, thereby broadening participation.  

---

**4. Injury Prevention Strategies**  
Injury prevention in playgrounds is multifaceted, involving both equipment design and environmental factors. Ergonomically informed design uses materials that absorb impact, rounded edges to prevent lacerations, and non-slip surfaces to reduce falls. Fall zones beneath elevated structures are often surfaced with engineered wood fiber, poured-in-place rubber, or synthetic turf, all compliant with impact attenuation criteria [3]. Equipment spacing is critical to prevent collisions, and moving components such as merry-go-rounds or seesaws must be balanced to reduce abrupt motion that could result in injury. Additionally, signage and age-appropriate labeling support safe usage by aligning equipment with developmental capabilities.  

---

**5. Integration of Ergonomics into Design Process**  
The design process benefits from early-stage ergonomic assessments, including prototyping with scaled models and user testing with representative age groups. Anthropometric data should inform dimensions, reach ranges, and grip diameters. Designers must also consider cognitive ergonomics—ensuring that equipment operation is intuitive and that hazards are perceptible to children. Collaboration among engineers, child development specialists, and safety inspectors ensures that ergonomic principles are embedded throughout the design lifecycle.  

---

**6. Future Directions and Policy Considerations**  
Emerging trends in playground ergonomics emphasize adaptability, allowing equipment to be reconfigured to meet evolving community needs. Digital tools, such as virtual simulations, can predict user interaction patterns and identify potential hazards before installation. Policymakers are encouraged to integrate ergonomic evaluation criteria into funding and procurement processes, ensuring that new playground installations meet both safety and accessibility benchmarks.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Ergonomic design in public playground equipment plays a pivotal role in safeguarding children’s wellbeing while fostering inclusive and engaging environments. Compliance with safety standards, incorporation of universal design features, and proactive injury prevention strategies collectively contribute to the creation of playgrounds that are both safe and accessible. Continued interdisciplinary research and policy support are essential to advance ergonomic best practices in public recreational spaces.  

---

The Australian case of compact cities derives from a study by Bunker.  [34]
It provides a commentary on urban development strategies used in Australia. To
begin with, Australia has very low population density because of its extensive
availability of space and its relatively low population.  [34]  However,
beginning in 2000, Australia adopted the compact city model for all its urban
planning. Planners adopted this development philosophy because projections
showed that the growth in Australia's largest cities was expected to be high
over the next decade.  [34]  In adopting the compact city model, Australian
planners set their development objectives to limit urban sprawl; to promote
infill, renewal, and redevelopment; to increase dwelling type diversity; to
diversify economic activity in communities; to motivate development to remain
close to the economic diversity; to encourage residents to use public
transportation; and to inspire residents to walk or cycle instead of driving
cars (13). Since 2000, Australia's growth patterns have followed these
objectives with positive outcomes. Not only are fossil fuel reduction
objectives being met, but compact community members are adopting more active
lifestyles, enhancing public health.  [34]  This suggests that by planning to
make urban communities self-sustaining, compact city planners can meet their
objectives.

majority of the Group’s emissions profile, SAF is the only viable
technology/decarbonisation option available across all of our operations.

approximately 60 per cent by 2050.

the US - as governments and industry work together to find ways to steadily
decarbonise the aviation sector through government fuel subsidies, SAF
blending mandates, financial incentives (subsidies and tax incentives) and
additional project-based funding such as capital grants and loans.

industry, including our $400 million Climate Fund, and Corporate SAF program.

Let the sunshine in. If your home sometimes fee﻿ls shuttered and gloomy, some simple changes can help. By inviting more natural light into a living space, you’ll create a lighter atmosphere and warm the interior.​ “Having a space that feels bright and airy creates almost an effervescence in the home that creates its own energy,” says Nicole Gibbons, an interior designer at Nicole Gibbons Studio in New York City.​ Beyond aesthetics, you may also notice a change in well-being.​ “Sunlight increases the amount of serotonin in our brains, and this is what makes us humans happy,” says Richard Hess, a designer in architecture, interiors and furniture for 22 years and director of career services at the NewSchool of Architecture and Design in San Diego. “It is scientifically proven that sunlight (vitamin D) elevates our moods daily” and decreases anxiety.​ As an added bonus, bringing in more natural light may reduce the amount of electricity used for artificial light, resulting in energy conservation and lowering your home's total energy costs by as much as one-third, according to the National Institute of Building Sciences. An integrated design approach called “daylighting” that's used in construction and remodeling﻿ can also be incorporated into an existing home. It combines well-positioned windows and skylights with blinds or shades to reduce glare during the day, along with artificial lighting to provide sufficient ambient lighting at night. ​ Here are 10 ways to bring more natural light indoors:​ ### 1\. Reconsider window treatments​ The amount of sunlight entering through windows depends on the type of window covering used. Liners on curtains or drapes help keep out the cold, but also block sunlight. Gibbons is a big fan of sun shades, which are made of a reflective material to repel heat and strong sun, but still let in some light. In warmer months, consider sheer curtains —on their own or layered over shades or under drapes. If privacy isn’t a concern, you live on an upper floor or face a grand view, you may be able to skip window treatments all together.​ ### 2\. Paint walls light colors​ A home’s interior colors play a role in the flow of natural light. Gibbons, who is also the founder and CEO of the paint site Clare, recommends using a lighter color palette to help reflect light and brighten spaces where sunlight is absent or limited. Look for paint colors with a light reflectan﻿ce value of 70 or higher. That information can be found on the back of a paint chip card or online. On the LRV scale of zero to 100, a higher number means the paint reflects more light; a lower number absorbs more light. Gibbons likes neutral, warm colors like whites, beiges and pale blues, grays and greens for interior walls.​ Gibbons also suggests using an eggshell paint finish because it’s “matte enough so it doesn’t have an obvious sheen but has enough gloss to be wiped down.” A higher sheen may create a glare. For more color, paint one wall — such as behind your bed or sofa — in a different, bolder color or add color with movable accessories like pillows and curtains.​ ### 3\. Keep the ceiling white​ The color and type of paint on a room’s ceiling can make a difference. Most people like white to create a sense of space. Gibbons recommends using a flat white finish to avoid glare from a light fixture creating a halo effect on the ceiling.​ ### 4\. Use mirrors to reflect light​ “Mirrors are a great trick for reflecting light,” Gibbons says. A mirror placed at the end of a hallway or in a corner opposite a window can bounce sunlight or light from an artificial light source around a room.​

## Install Bugproof Barriers Gangloff-Kaufmann advises using fine mesh screens in all open windows and doors. This allows cross-breezes to enter your house, but the screens’ openings are too small for mosquitoes to penetrate. Consider screens in your porch as well. “Screens are simply the best mosquito-control device you can find,” she says. “They were one of the original forms of home pest control, and for good reason.” If you already have screens, check the seals around the edges and use a patching kit to repair any tears to keep mosquitoes away. ## Eliminate Standing Water “Mosquitoes’ larvae develop in water,” Gangloff-Kaufmann says, “and they can do it in even the small amount of water that would fit in a bottle cap.” So to get rid of mosquitoes in your yard, it’s imperative to empty outdoor water toys and remove wheelbarrows and other outdoor gear that can catch water after a rainfall. Keep your gutters and drain lines clear of debris—clogged leaves and branches can cause water to pool. If your lawn has uneven terrain or divots, fill them with topsoil and plant grass seed. Left alone, any dips will collect water during each rainfall and provide a potential breeding ground. In a mere four days, eggs laid in water mature into nymphs, meaning if it rains on a Monday, you shouldn’t wait until the weekend to get rid of standing water. ## Keep Your Yard Neat Use a lawn mower, a string trimmer, or even a chainsaw to cut back high grass, brush, and tree limbs. “On hot days, mosquitoes favor cooler spots in the shade,” Gangloff-Kaufmann says. By minimizing tall grass or limbs that cast shadows on your yard, you make the habitat immediately surrounding your home much less appealing to mosquitoes. Letting more sun in also helps dry up any residual wet spots. The battery push mower, string trimmer, and chainsaw below are top-scoring models in CR’s tests. ## Use Fans CR has tested three methods for controlling mosquito activity in a large area: citronella candles, an oscillating pedestal fan, and a battery-powered area diffuser that emitted geraniol, a natural repellent derived from plants. We found that the fan is far more effective than citronella candles or the geraniol diffuser. In fact, our tests showed that the fan reduced mosquito landings by 45 to 65 percent for folks sitting nearby. “There’s a reason you see porch fans in mosquito-rich areas like the tropics,” Gangloff-Kaufmann says. She says that while a fan makes it more difficult for mosquitoes to fly against the steady breeze, it also helps disperse the carbon dioxide we emit when we breathe—a good thing because mosquitoes use carbon dioxide as a guide to finding humans when they’re looking to feed. ## Dress Appropriately To keep mosquitoes from biting you, wear long sleeves, pants, socks, and closed-toe shoes. This is especially important when you’re outdoors for a long stretch of time. It’s also wise to avoid tight-fitting clothes, because mosquitoes can penetrate them. Forgo dark-colored clothes and scented products, too, because these attract mosquitoes.

# Keeping the Heat Alive: Care and Preservation of Cast Iron Radiators in Heritage Homes

Cast iron radiators are more than just functional heating units; they are part of the architectural fabric of many heritage properties. Their distinctive appearance and robust construction lend a sense of authenticity to period interiors, while their ability to hold and radiate heat makes them a practical choice. Yet, without attentive upkeep, these stalwart fixtures can lose efficiency, succumb to corrosion, or fall into disrepair. The following guide outlines practical methods to enhance the efficiency and lifespan of cast iron radiators, blending technical care with aesthetic restoration to ensure they remain both beautiful and effective.

## Routine Maintenance for Optimal Performance

Regular maintenance is the foundation of radiator efficiency. Dust and debris tend to gather in the folds and crevices of cast iron columns, impeding heat transfer. A seasonal cleaning ritual—ideally at the start and end of each heating period—can make a measurable difference. Soft brushes or microfibre cloths work well for dry dusting, while a damp cloth with mild soap can remove stubborn grime. Avoid abrasive pads or harsh chemicals, as these can damage the finish.

Bleeding the radiator to remove trapped air is another essential step. Air pockets reduce the circulating hot water volume, lowering heat output. Using a radiator key, open the bleed valve slightly until water appears, then close it firmly. This simple task keeps the system running efficiently and helps to balance heat distribution throughout the property.

## Preventing Corrosion from the Inside Out

Corrosion is the chief enemy of cast iron radiators, and it can occur both externally and internally. Internally, oxygen ingress into the heating system water can lead to rust formation, particularly if the system has small leaks or is frequently topped up. Installing a high-quality inhibitor fluid in the system helps to neutralise corrosive elements, extending the radiator’s life. Periodically testing the inhibitor concentration ensures ongoing protection.

Externally, moisture and fluctuating temperatures can cause paint to crack, allowing rust to form on exposed metal. Inspecting the radiator surface annually for chips or scratches in the paintwork allows for prompt touch-ups. If rust spots are found, they should be gently sanded back to clean metal, primed with a rust-inhibiting primer, and repainted with a heat-resistant finish.

## Balancing Efficiency with Authenticity

Older radiators may have layers of paint applied over decades, sometimes obscuring the crisp details of their casting. Stripping back these layers—using a safe, non-caustic stripping method—can reveal the original craftsmanship, but should be followed by proper priming and painting to protect the bare metal. Colour choice can enhance the heritage aesthetic; deep, muted tones often complement period décor while still allowing the radiator to be a visual feature.

Efficiency upgrades need not compromise authenticity. For example, thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) can be fitted discreetly, enabling room-by-room temperature control without altering the radiator’s appearance. Likewise, insulating pipework in less visible areas reduces heat loss while maintaining original layouts.

## Professional Servicing and System Care

While much of the maintenance can be handled by the homeowner, periodic professional servicing is advisable. A heating engineer can flush the system to remove sludge build-up, check for leaks, and ensure pumps and valves are operating correctly. In heritage properties, where heating systems may have been adapted over many years, these inspections can prevent minor issues from escalating.

If the property’s boiler or heating source is upgraded, ensuring compatibility with existing radiators is critical. Cast iron units operate best with steady, moderate water temperatures, so any new system should be configured to avoid rapid temperature fluctuations that can stress the metal.

## Conclusion

Cast iron radiators have earned their place in heritage homes through decades—sometimes centuries—of service. By combining diligent cleaning, corrosion prevention, and sympathetic restoration, owners can preserve both their function and their charm. In doing so, these radiators remain a testament to the enduring value of traditional craftsmanship, providing warmth and character well into the future. 

Caring for them is not merely maintenance; it is stewardship of a living piece of the property’s history. With thoughtful attention, the gentle heat and timeless presence of a cast iron radiator can continue to grace heritage interiors for generations to come.

**From Field to Famine: The Story of Potatoes in Ireland**  

Few crops have shaped a nation’s history as profoundly as the humble potato did in Ireland. Introduced from the Americas in the late 16th century, the potato quickly became a staple food due to its adaptability to the Irish climate, high caloric yield per acre, and suitability for small-scale subsistence farming. Over the centuries, it wove itself into the fabric of rural life, influencing not only diet but also patterns of land use, social structures, and cultural traditions.  

**Early Cultivation and Cultural Integration**  
Before the industrial era, Irish agriculture was characterized by small plots and tenant farming. The potato’s resilience in poor soils and its ability to thrive in damp conditions made it a natural fit. Farmers relied on manual labor, using simple tools such as spades to plant and harvest. Seed potatoes were often saved from the previous year’s crop, and planting followed seasonal rhythms tied to local festivals and weather patterns.  

Potatoes became central to the daily diet across much of the rural population. They were boiled, baked, or mashed, and often served alongside milk or buttermilk, providing a complete and nourishing meal. This reliance was not just practical—it became cultural, with the potato appearing in folk songs, proverbs, and shared community meals.  

**The Fragile Foundation of a Staple**  
While the potato offered sustenance and security, it also introduced vulnerability. By the early 19th century, much of Ireland’s population depended almost exclusively on a single variety: the “Irish Lumper.” This monoculture meant that if disease struck, it could devastate the food supply. The reliance on tenant farming and small plots limited diversification, and political and economic structures left many families with little buffer against crop failure.  

**The Great Famine and Its Aftermath**  
In the mid-1840s, potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) swept across Ireland. Within just a few growing seasons, the blight destroyed most of the potato crop. The consequences were catastrophic: widespread hunger, disease, and death. Between 1845 and 1852, Ireland lost approximately one million people to starvation and illness, while another million emigrated, primarily to North America and Britain.  

The famine fundamentally altered Irish society. Depopulation changed rural communities, leaving abandoned cottages and fields. Families were torn apart by emigration, and the cultural landscape shifted as those who left carried with them traditions, language, and memories of home. The potato, once a symbol of sustenance, became a reminder of fragility and loss.  

**Migration and Cultural Transmission**  
Irish emigrants brought their agricultural knowledge and culinary traditions to new lands. Potatoes continued to feature in their diets abroad, adapted to local varieties and growing conditions. In cities like Boston and New York, potato-based dishes became part of Irish-American identity, connecting immigrant communities to their heritage.  

Migration also influenced Ireland itself. Remittances from abroad supported surviving relatives, and returning migrants brought back new ideas about farming, politics, and society. The memory of the famine reinforced a cautionary awareness about dependence on a single crop, encouraging diversification in later agricultural practices.  

**Legacy in Modern Ireland**  
Today, potatoes remain a cherished part of Irish cuisine—whether in traditional colcannon, boxty, or simply boiled with a sprinkle of salt. Modern farming methods have reduced the risk of blight, and multiple varieties are cultivated to ensure resilience. Yet the historical lessons of the famine continue to shape agricultural policy and cultural consciousness.  

The story of Ireland’s potato cultivation is one of adaptation, innovation, and tragedy. It illustrates how a single crop can sustain a people while also exposing them to profound risk. The potato’s journey from South America to Irish soil, its rise as a staple, and its role in the Great Famine form a narrative that is deeply embedded in Ireland’s identity—a reminder of the delicate balance between nature, culture, and survival.

**Report: Environmental Impact of Paper Manufacturing and Emission Reduction through Pulp Processing Innovation**  

---

**Abstract**  
This report examines the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with the manufacturing of office-grade paper, with particular emphasis on the pulp processing stage. By analyzing conventional mechanical and chemical pulping methods alongside emerging low-energy and closed-loop processing techniques, the report evaluates potential reductions in carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other GHG outputs. Findings indicate that targeted changes in energy sourcing, fiber preparation, and chemical recovery can produce measurable environmental benefits without compromising product quality.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Paper manufacturing remains a significant industrial contributor to global GHG emissions, driven largely by energy-intensive pulp preparation and bleaching operations. Office supply paper, typically produced to high brightness and smoothness standards, requires substantial mechanical and chemical treatment of raw fibers, often sourced from wood or recycled paper streams. The environmental footprint of these processes is shaped by fuel type, energy efficiency, and waste management practices. This report focuses on the pulp processing stage, where innovative techniques hold the greatest promise for emission reductions.

---

**2. Conventional Pulp Processing and Emissions Profile**  
Traditional pulp manufacturing relies on either mechanical pulping—using grinding or refining to separate fibers—or chemical pulping, which employs solutions such as sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide (kraft process) to break down lignin. Both methods consume large amounts of electricity and/or heat, often generated from fossil fuels.  

Key emission sources include:  

- **Electricity consumption** for mechanical refining, contributing indirect CO₂ emissions based on the local grid mix.  
- **Direct fuel combustion** in chemical pulping for steam generation, releasing CO₂, nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂).  
- **Bleaching stages**, which may involve chlorine-based agents, producing chlorinated organic compounds with environmental persistence.  

According to industry life-cycle assessments, pulp processing can account for 40–60% of total GHG emissions in the paper production chain [1].

---

**3. Emerging Low-Emission Pulp Techniques**  

**3.1 Energy-Efficient Mechanical Refining**  
Advances in refiner plate design and process control have reduced the specific energy demand per tonne of pulp. Variable frequency drive systems and optimized feed rates can lower electricity consumption by up to 25%, directly decreasing associated CO₂ emissions in regions reliant on fossil-based electricity generation.  

**3.2 Enzymatic Pre-Treatment**  
The use of cellulase and hemicellulase enzymes before mechanical refining weakens fiber bonds, enabling reduced mechanical energy input. Trials have shown total energy savings of 15–20% while maintaining fiber integrity.

**3.3 Closed-Loop Chemical Recovery in Kraft Mills**  
Modern recovery boilers and evaporators reclaim cooking chemicals and generate process steam from biomass residues. This shift from fossil fuels to renewable black liquor combustion can significantly reduce net GHG emissions, with some mills achieving near carbon-neutral energy balances.

**3.4 Oxygen and Ozone Bleaching**  
Replacing chlorine compounds with oxygen or ozone reduces harmful by-products and lowers the energy required for effluent treatment. These methods also allow for shorter bleaching sequences, further decreasing energy demand.

---

**4. Quantitative Impact of Technique Adoption**  
A model comparison between conventional and optimized pulp processing for office paper production (baseline: 500,000 tonnes/year) demonstrates the following potential reductions:  

- **Electricity-related CO₂**: 30,000 tonnes/year decrease through mechanical energy efficiency measures.  
- **Steam-related CO₂**: 45,000 tonnes/year decrease via biomass-based chemical recovery systems.  
- **Process-related GHGs**: 5,000 tonnes/year reduction by eliminating chlorine bleaching agents.  

These figures assume regional grid emission factors of 0.5 kg CO₂/kWh and fossil steam generation replaced with biomass combustion yielding near-zero fossil CO₂ emissions.

---

**5. Implementation Considerations**  
While technical feasibility is established, adoption rates depend on capital investment capacity, regulatory incentives, and market demand for environmentally certified office paper. Integration of new processing techniques requires workforce training, process redesign, and quality assurance testing to ensure compliance with ISO brightness and smoothness standards.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
The pulp processing stage in office paper manufacturing offers substantial opportunities for GHG emission reductions through energy efficiency, renewable energy integration, and chemical substitution. By transitioning to advanced mechanical refining, enzymatic pre-treatment, closed-loop chemical recovery, and non-chlorine bleaching, manufacturers can achieve significant environmental gains. These measures not only align with sustainability goals but also position producers competitively in markets increasingly sensitive to carbon footprints.

---

**References**

[2] European Pulp and Paper Research Institute. *Advances in Low-Energy Pulping Technologies*. 2021.  
[3] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. *Industrial Sector Greenhouse Gas Inventory*. 2020.

**The Timeless Allure: A Cultural History of Fragrance in Personal Care**  

From the earliest records of human civilization, the use of fragrance has been woven into the fabric of daily life, ritual, and identity. Long before modern perfumery and personal care industries emerged, ancient peoples crafted scented oils, powders, and unguents with remarkable artistry, imbuing them not only with pleasing aromas but also with deep symbolic meaning.  

**Fragrance in the Ancient World**  

In ancient Egypt, aromatic preparations were an essential part of both sacred and secular life. Priests burned kyphi—a complex blend of resins, herbs, honey, and wine—during temple rituals, believing the smoke carried prayers to the gods. Nobility and commoners alike anointed themselves with perfumed oils to mask the odors of the desert heat and to signify status. These oils were often stored in elegantly carved alabaster jars, which themselves became treasured objects of beauty.  

Across the Mediterranean in classical Greece, fragrance took on a philosophical dimension. The Greeks viewed scented oils as a form of bodily adornment, akin to fine clothing or jewelry. Perfume-makers, known as myropoioi, combined locally grown herbs with imported resins such as frankincense and myrrh. The preparation and application of these scents were regarded as an art form, reflecting harmony between nature and craftsmanship.  

**Ritual and Symbolism in the East**  

In India, the tradition of attar—natural perfume distilled from flowers, herbs, and spices—has roots stretching back millennia. Attars were used in religious ceremonies, applied to the body, and even infused into textiles. The scent of sandalwood, for example, was associated with purity and spiritual elevation, making it a staple in Hindu and Buddhist rituals. The production of attar required meticulous distillation processes, often passed down through generations, preserving both technique and cultural heritage.  

Similarly, in ancient China, fragrance was intertwined with the concept of qi, the vital life force. Incense and aromatic balms were used to create environments conducive to meditation and scholarly pursuits. The "Four Arts" of the Chinese literati—music, chess, calligraphy, and painting—were often accompanied by the subtle presence of fragrance, which was believed to sharpen the mind and elevate the soul.  

**Medieval and Renaissance Refinement**  

As trade routes expanded, so did the palette of available scents. In the Islamic Golden Age, perfumers in cities like Baghdad and Damascus perfected distillation techniques, introducing alcohol-based perfumes that allowed for greater variety and longevity of scent. Fragrance became a marker of sophistication, with courtly etiquette prescribing its use before audiences with rulers or during social gatherings.  

By the European Renaissance, perfumery had become intertwined with fashion and politics. Italian and French artisans crafted elaborate pomanders—small, perforated containers filled with aromatic substances—that were worn or carried to ward off illness and display wealth. The creation of these fragrances was celebrated as a fusion of science and artistry, blending botanical knowledge with aesthetic sensibilities.  

**Artistry Beyond Utility**  

What emerges from this historical tapestry is a clear understanding: fragrance in personal care was never merely functional. It was a language of symbols, a medium for expressing devotion, status, and identity. The vessels, techniques, and rituals surrounding scent were as important as the aromas themselves, reflecting the values and aesthetics of their cultures.  

From the alabaster jars of Egypt to the gilded perfume flacons of Versailles, the crafting of fragrance has always been a story of human creativity and cultural meaning. Each blend told a tale—of the land from which its ingredients came, of the hands that prepared it, and of the people who wore it in moments both ordinary and extraordinary.  

In tracing this lineage, we see that the allure of fragrance lies not only in its ability to please the senses, but also in its power to connect us to traditions, to artistry, and to the intangible essence of human experience. The scented oils and powders of the past remind us that personal care, at its most profound, is a reflection of the cultures that nurture it.

**Hemp in Ancient Medicine and Ritual: Historical Overview**  

**Introduction**  
Hemp (*Cannabis sativa*) has occupied a notable place in human culture for millennia, valued not only for its fibrous stalks but also for its seeds, oils, and medicinal properties. Archaeological and textual evidence attests to its widespread use in ancient civilizations across Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Europe. This entry examines the role of hemp as a medicinal ingredient in traditional remedies and ceremonial contexts, tracing its evolution from revered botanical to regulated commodity.

**Early Medicinal Applications**  
The earliest recorded medicinal use of hemp appears in Chinese sources dating to the early third millennium BCE. The *Shennong Bencao Jing* (“Divine Farmer’s Classic of Materia Medica”), compiled during the Han dynasty but drawing from earlier traditions, describes hemp seeds as a treatment for constipation, menstrual disorders, and other ailments. In these contexts, the seeds and seed oil were prized for their nutritive and emollient qualities, while preparations from leaves and flowers were sometimes employed for analgesic or sedative purposes.

In the Indian subcontinent, hemp was integrated into the Ayurvedic system under the name *bhanga*. Texts such as the *Sushruta Samhita* and *Bhavaprakasha* detail its use in relieving pain, stimulating appetite, and easing digestive complaints. Hemp-based concoctions were often combined with spices, milk, and other herbs to balance its perceived energetic properties according to Ayurvedic theory.

**Ceremonial and Spiritual Roles**  
Beyond its therapeutic applications, hemp held ceremonial significance in several ancient cultures. In India, *bhanga* preparations were consumed during religious festivals such as Holi and Shivaratri, symbolizing spiritual communion and purification. The psychoactive potential of certain hemp varieties was viewed as a means to achieve altered states conducive to meditation or ritual practice.

In Central Asia and among early Scythian tribes, archaeological discoveries of hemp seeds and burned plant material in burial mounds suggest its use in funerary rites. Greek historian Herodotus described Scythians inhaling hemp vapors during communal ceremonies, which may have combined elements of mourning, celebration, and healing.

**Mediterranean and Near Eastern Traditions**  
Evidence from ancient Egypt points to the use of hemp fibers in textiles, but medicinal references, though sparse, indicate application of hemp seed oil for inflammation and possibly as a topical remedy. In Assyrian medical tablets, certain plant preparations that scholars believe to be hemp were prescribed for neurological conditions and to ward off evil spirits—reflecting the intertwined nature of medicine and magic in Mesopotamian practice.

Greek and Roman authors, including Dioscorides and Galen, mention hemp primarily for its industrial utility, but they also note its medicinal uses. Dioscorides’ *De Materia Medica* records that hemp seeds could diminish sexual desire and were employed to treat earaches when boiled in water.

**Legal and Cultural Shifts**  
Throughout antiquity and into the medieval period, hemp maintained a dual identity as both a utilitarian crop and a medicinal resource. However, its regulation varied considerably. In some regions, psychoactive strains were restricted to ritual use under priestly supervision; in others, hemp was freely cultivated and traded.

From the late medieval era onward, shifts in legal status began to emerge, often tied to broader concerns about intoxication and social order. Islamic jurisprudence generally prohibited intoxicants, yet hemp derivatives such as hashish became prevalent in certain locales, leading to intermittent bans and enforcement campaigns. In Europe, hemp cultivation was encouraged for naval rope and canvas, while medicinal applications persisted quietly in herbal traditions.

**Modern Reassessment**  
By the nineteenth century, Western medical interest in hemp resurged, with physicians experimenting with cannabis extracts to treat pain, insomnia, and spasms. These uses were documented in pharmacopeias across Europe and North America. However, the twentieth century brought comprehensive legal restrictions in many countries, largely conflating industrial hemp with psychoactive cannabis. This curtailed its medicinal use and limited research, despite its long historical record.

In recent decades, changing laws and renewed scientific inquiry have led to a re-examination of hemp’s therapeutic potential, particularly its non-psychoactive constituents such as cannabidiol (CBD). While modern contexts differ greatly from ancient ceremonial and medicinal practices, the historical continuum underscores hemp’s enduring significance in human health and culture.

**Conclusion**  
Hemp’s medicinal and ritual roles in ancient civilizations reflect a complex interplay of practical utility, spiritual symbolism, and evolving legal frameworks. From early Chinese and Indian remedies to Scythian funerary rites and Greco-Roman herbalism, hemp’s history demonstrates its versatility and resilience as a plant of considerable cultural and therapeutic value. The shifts in perception and regulation over centuries provide essential context for understanding its place in both past and present medical traditions.

Deodorizing: Baking Soda’s deodorization power is a result of its ability to neutralize odors, rather than just covering up odors with perfumes. Most unpleasant odors come from either strong acids (like sour milk) or strong bases (spoiled fish). Baking Soda deodorizes by bringing both acidic and basic odor molecules into a neutral, more odor-free state. Use Baking Soda as a personal deodorant for underarms and feet, and as a household deodorant on carpets, upholstery and in the fridge and freezer. Baking Soda can also deodorize when it’s dissolved in water. So you can use Baking Soda as a mouthwash to neutralize garlic breath, as a diaper soak to neutralize that ‘ammonia’ smell (basic) and to deodorize plastic food containers that have absorbed that pickle or sauerkraut smell (acidic). Industrially, Baking Soda is used for odor control of sewage disposal plants and around barn and feedlots. Leavening: The most universal use of Baking Soda is for baking in which Baking Soda is used to promote leavening. Leavening increases the surface area of dough or batter by causing it to rise and become light and porous. The most common leavening agent is carbon dioxide, a gas that is produced by a chemical reaction with the use of Baking Soda, baking powder or yeast in a recipe. Baking Soda yields the carbon dioxide for leavening when it’s heated. When used as a leavening agent, Baking Soda also reacts with acidic ingredients to render a neutral, tasteless residue. Common examples of these acidic ingredients include sour milk, buttermilk, molasses, cream of tartar, lemon juice and the acidic substances in baking powder. Baking Soda has been used by generations of good cooks who have trusted our unwavering standard of purity since 1846...from our great-grandmothers, to our grandmothers and now to us. Buffering: Because of its chemical makeup, Baking Soda has unique capabilities as a buffer. Buffering is the maintenance of a stable pH balance, or acid-alkali balance. As a buffer, Baking Soda tends to cause acid solutions to become more basic and to cause basic solutions to become more acid, bringing both solutions to a stable pH around 8.1 (slightly basic) on the pH scale. A buffer also resists pH change in a solution, in this case maintaining a pH of 8.1. In this way Baking Soda can be used as an antacid in the human digestive system, neutralizing acids from acid indigestion and heartburn and relieving the associated discomfort. (See directions for this use on the Baking Soda box.) When used as a paste on skin or in the bath, Baking Soda soothes the irritation of poison ivy, insect bites, sunburn, and prickly heat. The natural buffering of Baking Soda also means that it’s a safe and natural way to maintain appropriate pH levels in pools, where stable pH keeps water quality at its best, and in septic tanks, where stable pH provides a healthy environment for the beneficial bacteria that break down wastes. Industrially, Baking Soda is used in sewage treatment facilities for its ability to maintain favorable pH levels. Fire Extinguishing: Baking Soda is effective as a fire extinguisher for grease and electrical fires. When Baking Soda is heated it releases carbon dioxide (just as when dough rises) and produces water. Since carbon dioxide is heavier than air and does not support combustion like oxygen does, it smothers the fire while the water that is formed cools the fire to below the ignition temperature. Unlike any other household chemical, Baking Soda both cools and smothers a fire. Many homes have Baking Soda readily available as a first step in fighting kitchen, garage and car fires -- then call the Fire Department. Many commercial fire extinguishers, including dry chemical and foam, contain Baking Soda.

**Optimizing Lettuce Production in Urban Vertical Hydroponic Systems: Nutrient Delivery and LED Lighting Configurations**  

---

**Abstract**  
Urban agriculture increasingly relies on vertical hydroponic systems to address constraints in space, resource efficiency, and year-round production. This study examines the optimization of lettuce (*Lactuca sativa*) yields in controlled indoor environments through the integration of precise nutrient delivery protocols and tailored LED lighting configurations. Experimental trials compared multiple nutrient solution concentrations and spectral compositions of LED arrays to determine their effects on biomass accumulation, leaf morphology, and nutrient uptake efficiency. Results indicate that balanced macronutrient provision coupled with a red-blue dominant light spectrum at specific photon flux densities significantly enhanced growth rates and yield consistency. The findings provide a framework for maximizing lettuce production in urban hydroponic installations while minimizing input waste.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Urban vertical hydroponics offers potential solutions to challenges of food security, land scarcity, and environmental impact by enabling high-density cultivation in limited spaces [1,2]. Lettuce is a preferred candidate for such systems due to its relatively short growth cycle, high market demand, and responsiveness to controlled environmental parameters [3]. Two critical factors influencing productivity in vertical hydroponic systems are nutrient delivery efficiency and light spectrum optimization. Nutrient delivery must be precisely calibrated to meet plant requirements without excess, thereby reducing resource waste and potential system imbalances [4]. Similarly, light quality and quantity directly affect photosynthetic efficiency, morphogenesis, and overall yield [5].  

---

**2. Materials and Methods**  

**2.1 System Design**  
The study was conducted in a multi-tier vertical hydroponic installation consisting of six stacked growing levels within a climate-controlled chamber. Each tier was equipped with independent nutrient delivery lines and programmable LED lighting arrays.  

**2.2 Plant Material and Growth Conditions**  
Lettuce cultivar ‘Grand Rapids’ was selected for uniformity and rapid growth. Seeds were germinated in rockwool cubes and transplanted into NFT (nutrient film technique) channels after 10 days. Ambient temperature was maintained at 22 ± 1°C with relative humidity between 60–70%.  

**2.3 Nutrient Delivery Treatments**  
Three nutrient solution regimes were tested:  
- **Low concentration**: 75% of standard commercial hydroponic recommendations.  
- **Standard concentration**: 100% recommended formulation.  
- **High concentration**: 125% recommended formulation.  

Nutrient solutions were monitored daily for electrical conductivity (EC) and pH, adjusted to maintain EC within ±0.1 mS/cm and pH between 5.8–6.2.  

**2.4 LED Lighting Configurations**  
Three lighting treatments were applied:  
- **RB Spectrum**: 70% red (660 nm) and 30% blue (450 nm).  
- **Full Spectrum**: Broad emission including red, blue, green, and far-red wavelengths.  
- **Enhanced Blue**: 50% blue, 50% red.  

Photon flux density (PFD) levels were set at 200, 250, and 300 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ for comparison.  

**2.5 Data Collection**  
Growth metrics included fresh and dry biomass, leaf area index (LAI), chlorophyll content (SPAD values), and nutrient uptake efficiency calculated from solution depletion rates. Statistical analysis was conducted using ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc test at p < 0.05.  

---

**3. Results**  

**3.1 Nutrient Delivery Efficiency**  
The standard concentration treatment produced the highest mean fresh biomass (285 g per plant) with minimal nutrient residuals in the solution, indicating efficient uptake. The high concentration treatment showed increased residual nitrate levels, suggesting over-supply and potential leaching risks.  

**3.2 LED Spectrum Effects**  
The RB spectrum at 250 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ resulted in the greatest biomass accumulation and LAI, with leaves exhibiting optimal chlorophyll content and uniform morphology. Enhanced blue treatments yielded more compact plants with higher leaf thickness but reduced total biomass.  

**3.3 Interaction Effects**  
Significant interactions were observed between nutrient concentration and light spectrum. The combination of standard nutrient delivery with RB spectrum lighting at 250 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ produced a 17% higher yield compared to all other combinations.  

---

**4. Discussion**  
The findings reinforce the importance of aligning nutrient delivery rates with plant demand to avoid waste and maintain system balance [6]. Excessive nutrient concentrations did not translate to yield benefits and may increase operational costs and environmental impact in urban settings. Light spectrum optimization proved equally critical; red-blue dominant configurations supported photosynthetic efficiency while controlling plant morphology, consistent with previous reports [7]. The moderate PFD of 250 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ balanced energy input with plant productivity, suggesting diminishing returns at higher intensities.  

---

**5. Conclusion**  
Urban vertical hydroponic systems can achieve high and consistent lettuce yields by integrating precise nutrient management with optimized LED spectral configurations. The combination of standard nutrient concentrations and RB spectrum lighting at moderate PFD offers an effective balance between productivity and resource efficiency. Future research should explore dynamic lighting and nutrient modulation across growth stages to further refine system performance.  

---

**Green Playgrounds Take Root in Cities: A New Approach to Urban Cooling and Community Wellness**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

In cities across the country, a new kind of playground is emerging—one that blends fun with environmental stewardship. These eco-friendly play spaces are designed not only to entertain children but also to combat the effects of urban heat islands, a growing concern in densely built environments.  

Urban heat islands occur when concrete, asphalt, and other heat-retaining materials absorb and radiate warmth, pushing local temperatures higher than in surrounding rural areas. This phenomenon can strain energy resources, impact air quality, and pose health risks, especially for vulnerable populations. Architects, city planners, and community groups are now turning to passive design strategies in public spaces to help alleviate these effects.  

**Designing with Nature in Mind**  

One of the most striking features of the new playgrounds is the incorporation of plant-covered structures. These living installations—ranging from vertical gardens on play towers to pergolas draped in vines—provide shade, improve air quality, and create a more inviting atmosphere. The plants absorb sunlight, reducing surface heat, and their evapotranspiration helps cool the surrounding area.  

In several pilot projects, designers have used native plant species that require minimal irrigation, ensuring the greenery thrives without placing undue demand on water resources. The result is a play space that not only stays cooler on hot days but also fosters biodiversity in urban settings.  

**Recycled Materials for a Smaller Footprint**  

Alongside vegetation, the use of recycled and reclaimed materials has become a hallmark of these spaces. In one recently opened park in Portland, Oregon, climbing structures are built from repurposed timber, while playground flooring is made from recycled rubber tires. These choices reduce waste, lower the environmental impact of construction, and give the space a distinctive aesthetic—colorful, textured, and rich with character.  

Material selection also plays a role in temperature moderation. Lighter-colored surfaces reflect more sunlight, while porous materials allow rainwater to filter through, reducing runoff and helping maintain cooler ground temperatures.  

**Shaded Areas Improve Comfort and Safety**  

Shade is a critical component in the fight against heat stress, especially for children. New playground designs emphasize shaded zones not only over seating areas but also over play equipment itself. Large fabric canopies, tree plantings, and plant-covered shelters protect young visitors from direct sun exposure, reducing the risk of heat-related illnesses and making outdoor play more enjoyable year-round.  

In Dallas, a recently renovated playground features a mix of tall trees and tensile fabric structures that create pockets of cool air throughout the park. Parents report that their children can play longer without becoming overheated, and the shaded seating areas have become informal gathering spots for caregivers, fostering stronger community ties.  

**Benefits Beyond Cooling**  

While the primary goal of these designs is to mitigate heat, the benefits extend well beyond temperature control. Green playgrounds encourage physical activity in a safe, comfortable environment, which supports child health and development. Exposure to natural elements has been linked to reduced stress, improved mood, and better concentration in children.  

Communities also gain from the social aspects of these spaces. By creating inviting, accessible parks, cities can strengthen neighborhood connections and encourage civic pride. Volunteer groups often participate in planting and maintenance, giving residents a sense of ownership over their local environment.  

**Looking Ahead**  

Urban planners are watching closely as early adopters of these green playground concepts report positive outcomes. Data from several cities indicate a measurable drop in surface temperatures in and around the sites, along with increased park usage even during summer’s peak heat.  

Funding remains a challenge, as plant-covered structures and sustainable materials can carry higher upfront costs than conventional designs. However, advocates argue that long-term savings in health care, cooling energy, and stormwater management make these investments worthwhile.  

As climate pressures mount, the integration of passive environmental strategies into everyday public spaces is gaining momentum. For children, these playgrounds offer a cooler, healthier place to play; for communities, they represent a step toward more resilient, livable cities.  

In the words of one landscape architect involved in a recent project, “We’re not just building playgrounds—we’re creating microclimates that nurture both people and the planet.”  

With more municipalities exploring these designs, green playgrounds may soon become a familiar sight, offering shade, comfort, and beauty in the heart of the urban landscape.

**Global Asparagus Trade Faces Shifts Under Climate Change Pressures**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

Over the past decade, the international asparagus market has experienced significant fluctuations, with climate change emerging as a key driver of transformation in production hubs, trade flows, and consumer preferences. Once considered a niche export crop, asparagus has become emblematic of how shifting weather patterns and environmental pressures can ripple through global agricultural supply chains.  

**Production Centers Under Strain**  
Historically, Peru, China, and Mexico have dominated global asparagus exports, supplying fresh and processed products to Europe, North America, and Asia. However, increasingly erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, and prolonged droughts have begun to undermine yields in several of these regions. In Peru’s coastal valleys—long prized for their consistent climate—water scarcity linked to glacial retreat and reduced river flows has forced growers to invest in costly irrigation infrastructure or reduce planting areas. Similarly, northern Mexico has faced prolonged heat waves, pushing harvest dates earlier and shortening the productive season.  

China, the largest producer by volume, has encountered its own set of challenges, including shifts in precipitation patterns and soil degradation in key growing provinces. Producers there have reported difficulty meeting export quality standards, driving some overseas buyers to diversify sourcing.  

**Changing Trade Patterns**  
As traditional supply regions grapple with climate-related disruptions, new players have entered the asparagus market. Southern European countries, particularly Spain and Italy, have expanded production capacity, capitalizing on milder winters and investments in greenhouse cultivation. Meanwhile, emerging exporters in Africa—such as Kenya and South Africa—are attracting attention for their ability to deliver off-season harvests to European supermarkets.  

These shifts have altered trade flows, with importers increasingly spreading risk across multiple source countries. The once-dominant Peru-to-U.S. supply chain now competes with Mexican and domestic U.S. producers for market share, particularly during peak demand in spring. European retailers, similarly, have adjusted procurement strategies to account for potential weather-related supply shocks.  

**Tariff Adjustments and Policy Responses**  
Trade policy has also evolved in response to the changing production landscape. Several importing nations have reduced tariffs on asparagus from non-traditional suppliers to stabilize availability and prevent price spikes. In the European Union, temporary tariff relaxations for African exporters have encouraged diversification of sourcing. Conversely, some countries have imposed stricter phytosanitary requirements on imports from regions experiencing increased pest pressures due to warmer climates, adding complexity to trade logistics.  

Exporting nations are likewise revisiting their own policies. Peru has offered tax incentives for water-efficient farming technologies, while Mexico has sought bilateral agreements to secure long-term supply contracts despite seasonal yield variability.  

**Consumer Demand Trends**  
Climate change has not only disrupted supply; it has also influenced consumer behavior. In markets such as Germany, the United Kingdom, and Japan, heightened awareness of the environmental footprint of imported produce has spurred interest in locally grown asparagus, even when it means shorter availability windows. This shift has bolstered domestic producers in temperate regions, who can market their crops as fresher and more sustainable.  

At the same time, premium segments—such as organic or specialty varieties—have maintained strong growth, with buyers willing to pay higher prices for consistent quality despite weather-related constraints. Retailers have responded by investing in controlled-environment agriculture, including vertical farms and hydroponic systems, to ensure year-round supply.  

**Outlook**  
Analysts expect continued volatility in the global asparagus trade over the next decade. Climatic instability will likely accelerate the redistribution of production across latitudes, encouraging investment in adaptive cultivation practices and infrastructure. Trade agreements and tariff policies will remain fluid, shaped by the dual pressures of securing supply and meeting sustainability goals.  

For consumers, the asparagus market may become more segmented, with clear distinctions between locally produced seasonal offerings and imported products sourced from climate-resilient regions. For producers, success will hinge on agility—both in responding to environmental change and in navigating the evolving trade environment.  

In this context, the story of asparagus serves as a microcosm of broader agricultural challenges, illustrating how climate change is reshaping not only where food is grown but also how it moves across borders and reaches the plate.
